entries.title: In Scathing Ruling, Judge Extends Ban on Tree Cutting at Trump’s Golf Project
entries.summary: Judge Ana Reyes cited Dr. Seuss in issuing a temporary restraining order against changes to the East Potomac Golf Course.
entries.content:
A federal judge on Monday extended a ban on cutting down trees at East Potomac Golf Course in Washington, handing down a blistering opinion against President Donald Trump’s overhaul of the historic public course.

U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes chided federal prosecutors, jabbed at the president’s social media habits and likened the case to Dr. Seuss’ tree-loving Lorax in her 70-page opinion, which she mocked as “Lorax v. Once‑ler redux.”

“The Court earlier stated, ‘I am not the Lorax. I do not speak for the trees,’” Reyes wrote. “The Court still does not speak for the trees. It speaks only for the rule of law.”

The plaintiffs, the D.C. Preservation League, argue the government planned to “to destroy” East Potomac Golf Course and replace it with a championship-style course suitable for professional tournaments.

The Justice Department claimed there was no final decision on such a plan and that it was the National Park Service that would make the ultimate call.

“Rarely, if ever, has the United States Department of Justice urged a federal court not to believe the sitting President,” Reyes wrote. “Not to believe him that the secretary’s agency will destroy a historic golf course already on the land. Not to believe him that ‘Restoration work’ will begin ‘IMMEDIATELY!’ Not to believe him that the course ‘will be closed’ for over a year. Not to believe what the President has repeatedly told the American public.”

“And yet,” she added, “here we are.”

Reyes granted a preliminary injunction prohibiting the Trump administration from removing or damaging additional trees. Officials must also provide 10 business days’ written notice before making other irreversible changes to East Potomac Park while the lawsuit proceeds.

The decision extends protections Reyes first levied after the government cut down more than 400 trees on Oct. 10.

Trump has promoted the project as a potential venue for the U.S. Open and Ryder Cup, promising that the green would remain open to the public. Last week, right before a court hearing on the case, he announced that the existing course would close in November and would not reopen until 2028.

But Interior Department officials told the court that they had no official plans to close the park. The Justice Department said that the lawsuit was premature, despite evidence of public statements, designs and active construction work provided by the D.C. Preservation League.

“If, as DOJ insists, President Trump is wrong, Secretary Burgum can just say so,” she wrote, referring to Interior Secretary Doug Burgum. “He has not.”

The fight has become a flash point in Trump’s efforts to overhaul public spaces across D.C.

Rep. Jared Huffman of California, the top Democrat on the House Natural Resources Committee, revealed last month that the Park Service had awarded a contract for the work without notifying Congress.

Trump called Reyes a “crazed lunatic” last week, after the Justice Department failed to secure her recusal in the case.

In Monday’s opinion, Reyes emphasized that she had repeatedly declined to intervene before the October tree cutting, relying on government assurances that officials would provide meaningful notice before undertaking major changes.

She rejected arguments from the administration that the tree removal was routine maintenance, saying there was “no universe” in which the tree removal was intended as restoration work.

Reyes concluded that the D.C. Preservation League is likely to succeed in its arguments that government officials violated environmental policies in their renovation plan.

Democracy Forward President and CEO Skye Perryman, whose organization is co-counsel representing the plaintiffs, called the ruling “a big win that will rightly protect East Potomac Park from further irreparable harm,” according to The Associated Press. She added, in an email to the AP, that the move will stop activities “while the case continues, and we are eager to argue the case in court.”

entries.title: Wizards Fall to Hornets, 110-103
entries.content:
CHARLOTTE, N.C. (AP) — Brandon Miller scored a career-high 39 points, and the Charlotte Hornets beat the Washington Wizards 110-103 on Monday night for their third win in four games to open the season.

Starters Coby White (left calf) and Kon Knueppel (left hamstring) and top reserve Grant Williams (right hamstring) each have yet to play this season for the Hornets, who have managed their absences well so far.

Miller scored 27 points in the middle two quarters as Charlotte took control.

The fourth-year guard topped 30 points for the 14th time in his career and scored 30 in back-to-back games for the fourth time. A 2023 first-round pick out of Alabama, Miller a week ago signed a five-year, $209 million contract extension.

Naz Reid finished with 18 points and 12 rebounds for the Hornets, who had a seemingly comfortable 98-84 lead with 5:15 to play.

But the Wizards (2-2), who were seeking their first 3-1 start since the 2022-23 season, knocked down five 3-pointers down the stretch and got as close as 103-100 with 1:13 to play.

Miller hit a jumper and later made a free throw for his final three points to make it 106-100 with 38.3 seconds left.

Grayson Allen added 15 points and Moussa Diabate had 11 points and 17 rebounds for Charlotte.

Anthony Davis had 29 points and 10 rebounds, Trae Young scored 22 points and Kyshawn George added 20 points for Washington. Wizards forward Justin Champagnie suffered a right foot injury in the first quarter and did not return.

Washington was again without A.J. Dybantsa, the No. 1 overall pick in the 2026 NBA draft, whose debut has been delayed by a sprained left ankle.

Davis' personal win streak against Charlotte ended. The Hornets had lost 10 straight games in which the oft-injured Davis had played against them, dating to March 2016.

entries.title: Appeals Court Rejects Trump Administration’s Emergency Appeal Over California Ballots
entries.summary: The case lands back at a U.S. district court, which is set Tuesday to weigh a preliminary injunction on sequestering 20,000 ballots.
entries.content:
A federal appeals court on Monday dismissed the Trump administration’s emergency motion seeking to force California to sequester 20,000 mail ballots from suspected noncitizen voters, chastising the government for rushing to appeal before a trial judge could issue an initial ruling.

The 2-1 decision from a panel of the 9th Circuit Court of Appeals means the underlying lawsuit is not yet resolved and will be first handled in a lower court, with a hearing on a temporary injunction scheduled Tuesday before U.S. District Judge David Carter, just a week before Election Day.

“The United States’s claimed emergency, at least in part, is a self-constructed one,” the appellate court wrote in a decision that came after rare Sunday arguments.

The Trump administration sued election officials in California to set aside any mail ballots filled out by people on a list Trump administration alleges contains the names of more than 20,000 “likely” noncitizens it says are registered to vote in the state. The Justice Department asked Carter to stop the state from counting those ballots until immigration status checks were completed.

California officials have questioned the list’s reliability. A state review found that, among those with usable birthplace information, 38.9% were born in the United States.

The government initially asked Carter to rule by Nov. 3. Then, when he scheduled an Oct. 27 hearing on the request, the prosecutors abruptly demanded a ruling by noon the following day, giving him roughly 15 hours to levy his opinion.

When he did not rule, prosecutors filed an emergency appeal to the 9th Circuit Court of Appeals. The majority on a three-judge panel said the Trump administration “failed to allow the district court adequate opportunity to consider” their move to sequester the ballots.

The court did not rule on the merits of the case, though the judges individually hinted at what they thought about the Justice Department’s actions.

Judge Mark Bennett, a Trump appointee, said he had concerns about the provenance of the voter list and warned that the government’s efforts could leave eligible voters disenfranchised and jeopardize Los Angeles County’s election operations.

Judge Patrick Bumatay, another Trump appointee, dissented. He argued that immediate intervention was necessary because any ballots cast illegally would become impossible to identify once votes are being tabulated.

The case is unlikely to be decided in finality by Carter and could make its way to the U.S. Supreme Court before a final ruling is handed down, according to election law experts.

entries.title: Experts Warn Escalating Iran Strikes Could Bring Retaliation Rather Than a U.S. Victory
entries.summary: As Trump weighs fresh attacks, military analysts and former officials say the risks may outweigh the benefits.
entries.content:
President Donald Trump said he is weighing whether to strike Iran again or pursue a negotiated settlement, raising the prospect of a fresh American military campaign and questions about what another round of bombing could accomplish that months of intermittent fighting have not.

“Do I make a deal with them or do I finish them off? That’s the only question,” Trump said in a Sunday interview with Fox News, signaling he is still considering another major military operation.

The U.S. and Israeli militaries have reportedly developed plans for an intensive three-day bombing campaign against Iran, with an expanded target list that includes energy infrastructure and facilities vital to the Iranian economy. CNN reported that American forces could launch an operation within 96 hours of receiving Trump’s orders. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his team have openly advocated overthrowing Iran’s government.

But former U.S. officials and experts questioned whether another round of strikes could deliver the Trump administration’s elusive strategic victory. A successful campaign against Iran’s remaining missile forces, military installations or command infrastructure would not necessarily force its leaders to surrender or shatter the Islamic Republic’s security apparatus, told The Washington Sun.

And a broader campaign could expose U.S. troops and regional allies to retaliation, potentially pulling Washington into a more prolonged and destructive war.

Jason Campbell, a former Pentagon official now at the Middle East Institute, said U.S. military options appear confined to airstrikes, while Iran’s dispersed command structures have been designed to survive the destruction of military facilities and senior leaders.

“I fail to see how the United States and Israel are three or four days of strikes away from what would be a strategic-level change,” Campbell said.

Behnam Ben Taleblu, an Iran specialist at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies who has supported previous American military action against Iran, argued against new strikes. Trump has “a winning hand,” he said, by sticking with his naval blockade of the Strait of Hormuz and intensifying economic pressure.

“The president can box in Tehran more effectively and slow the Islamic Republic’s rebuild of its nuclear, missile and military programs, and drive the regime to have to expend a declining amount of capital on a greater series of things,” Taleblu said. “Rather than have Uncle Sam or Israel be blamed … you put the burden and the onus of escalation onto the regime.”

The Pentagon is preparing to reinforce its presence in the Middle East, with the 13th Marine Expeditionary Unit reportedly heading to the region, along with another aircraft carrier. Those deployments could add 10,000 to 15,000 sailors and Marines to the roughly 50,000 U.S. military personnel already in the region.

Military analysts said more ambitious objectives, including seizing Iranian territory or overthrowing the government, would require a major ground operation — far beyond the forces available in the region and what the administration has so far been willing to risk.

Analysts estimate that securing shipping through the Strait of Hormuz would require at least 100,000 troops to occupy hundreds of miles of Iranian coastline, extending some 30 miles inland to protect against Iranian missiles.

The operation would entail large-scale amphibious and airborne assaults along a marshy coastline with few suitable landing sites. American forces would have to assemble within range of Iranian missiles, then face conventional attacks and insurgent resistance once ashore, risking heavy casualties without a guaranteed result.

“Even if you wanted to do that, where on Earth in that region are you going to stage the sufficient forces to prepare for such an operation,” said Campbell, who recently war-gamed the scenario with military planners. “Because right now, Iran has either destroyed or made very unsafe pretty much every installation that the U.S. would potentially use for any kind of a major ground operation.”

Ben Connable, a former Marine officer and RAND Corporation military analyst now with the Battle Research Group, said another air campaign could weaken Iran’s conventional military without really changing the conflict. The U.S. hasn’t shown the appetite for the ground invasion needed to take out the Iranian government.

“I don't see any way around a ground invasion unless you're just planning on luck,” Connable said. “And luck in this case would be the Iranian economy collapses, or there's a revolt against the leadership, and that can't be predetermined.”

Connable also warned that Washington could stumble into a ground conflict without choosing one. A downed American aircraft could trigger a combat search-and-rescue operation involving hundreds of troops operating inside hostile territory.

Iranian officials, meanwhile, have warned that renewed attacks would not force Tehran to change its position.

"Recently, there has been talk of a new war, but I am already thinking about the post-war period,” Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Sunday during a televised event in Tehran, according to an Arab News translation. “Whether there is war or not, our policies remain the same."

Iran, meanwhile, has threatened to expand its retaliation beyond American military targets. Officials have warned that new strikes could trigger attacks on airports, pipelines, undersea internet cables and other civilian infrastructure across the Persian Gulf, as well as U.S. bases and warships.

Connable said he considers attacks on Gulf Arab states and commercial shipping particularly credible threats, because they are “less well defended than a warship” and because they could be used to “pump the price of oil back up again” and strengthen Tehran’s negotiating leverage.

Iranian officials have also suggested the war could expand. “Our strategy is ‘zero red lines,’” Mehdi Mohammadi, an adviser to Iran's nuclear negotiator, told The Guardian last week. “The war will continue longer and in a wider geographical area than the enemy anticipates.”

The threat is already prompting precautions. Axios reported that Jay Clayton, the director of national intelligence, warned Friday that Iran "substantially increased" its efforts to target American diplomats and officials in the Middle East and beyond, with lethal plots reaching "advanced stages.”

The State Department has ordered nonessential embassy personnel and their families to leave Saudi Arabia and has reduced staffing at other diplomatic posts in the region. The Pentagon withdrew about a dozen B-1 bombers from a British airbase this month following warnings of a possible Iranian-backed attack.

Connable warned of a threat that has yet to fully emerge: terrorist attacks by Iranian operatives or networks against Americans beyond the battlefield.

“That is a capacity they have; they have not demonstrated it,” Connable said. “The more desperate we make them, the more likely they are to resort to terrorism.”

entries.title: Three Big Questions for Jayden Daniels Coming Out of the Bye
entries.summary: It has been an up-and-down start for the Commanders’ third-year quarterback. We took a deeper look at the numbers.
entries.content:
The 2026 season was supposed to be a reset year for Jayden Daniels, after his incredible rookie year was followed by a mostly lost sophomore campaign. But the start to Year 3 has not been particularly smooth. Daniels missed two and a half games with a dislocated elbow that currently requires a brace. There have also been injuries across the offense, the latest being star wide receiver Terry McLaurin’s season-ending knee injury.

Still, we have enough game action to make an early evaluation of how Daniels is adjusting to the offense under new coordinator David Blough. Through Week 6, Daniels ranked 15th in the NFL in expected points added (EPA) per play and success rate, while he ranked 12th in ESPN’s QBR system — effectively measuring Daniels as a slightly-above-average quarterback through the first part of the season.

We took a closer look at how he has performed, with an eye towards what could be improved upon as the season unfolds.

Has He Been Effective Playing From Under Center?

This was one of the big talking points heading into the season. Part of the reason why Blough was hired as coordinator was to install an offense that could operate more frequently from under center, with the aim of opening up both the running and play-action games.

In the small sample we’ve seen from Daniels so far, the results haven’t been great. In shotgun, Daniels averages 0.12 EPA per play with a 44.5% success rate. When under center, he averages -0.22 EPA per play with a 40.9% success rate. Daniels only has 20 under-center dropbacks, but that’s also part of the issue. The lack of production there — and with Daniels clearly more comfortable playing out of shotgun — has stopped the offense from leaning into it more.

However, the run game improvement with Daniels on the field has been there. On 27 running back carries from under center with Daniels, the Commanders average 0.06 EPA per rush with a 48.1% success rate. From shotgun, the Commanders average -0.12 EPA per rush with a 31.6% success rate on 38 carries.

If Daniels can get more comfortable playing from under center during the second half of the season, the Commanders could see an uptick in their offensive performance.

Why Has He Struggled When Under Pressure?

Both the biggest improvement and decline from Daniels have to do with pressure. When Daniels hasn't been pressured this season, he’s been one of the best quarterbacks in the league statistically. His 0.55 EPA per play ranks second, only behind Lamar Jackson’s 0.72. He’s getting the ball out quickly (2.42 seconds to throw), and that has created open windows to throw. According to NFL Next Gen Stats, Daniels has the 12th-lowest rate of throws into a tight coverage window.

When not pressured, 53.9% of his throws have gone between 1-10 air yards. On a down-to-down basis, he’s been more willing than in previous seasons to take something underneath, get the completion and let his receivers try to run after the catch. In his first two seasons, just over 40% of Daniels’s passes went to that depth when not under pressure.

That isn’t to say Daniels has lacked risk-taking this season. When he’s gotten time to be clean in the pocket and rip it down the field, he’s made some nice throws. And his 3.5% completion percentage over expected is a career-high and 10th in the league.

The problems have come when he’s under pressure. Daniels ranks 28th in EPA per play under pressure, a far cry from his sixth-best ranking in 2024. Even though he has lowered his sack rate (7.9%) to a career low, his production has taken a dive when opposing pass rushes are able to throw him off schedule.

One reason? His throwaway rate (21.7%) when under pressure is the second-highest mark in the league. It’s possible that as he gets more comfortable in the offense, and in his return from injury, that his performance in this area could pick up. It’s difficult to believe a quarterback with Daniels’ athleticism would remain so poor under pressure.

How Can He Overcome the Loss of McLaurin?

One of the keys for Daniels heading into 2026 was reestablishing his connection with McLaurin. The duo was one of the league’s best in 2024, but never recaptured that magic in 2025. Now, with McLaurin out for the rest of the season, the Commanders will again be without their top quarterback and wide receiver on the field together.

The immediate answer should be more Antonio Williams. The third-round rookie has caught 10 of his 11 targets from Daniels for 145 yards. When paired with veteran Stefon Diggs, who has been the most-targeted receiver from Daniels and has been especially effective in the short-to-intermediate range, that’s not a bad 1-2 option. Adding either Treylon Burks or Dyami Brown to the two of them keeps an 11 personnel alignment (three receivers, one tight end, one running back) viable.

But the Commanders could also lean into heavier looks in 12 and 13 personnel to force defenses to play bigger. Over the past two weeks, Washington has sprinkled some of these plays in for big gains.

The ideal surroundings the Commanders may have wanted for Daniels haven’t played out, but the third-year quarterback is adapting and showing signs of the player who was one of the rising stars of the league as a rookie. Washington might not have the same team success in 2026 — although the NFC East remains wide open — but if Daniels takes a step forward in his development, there will be reason for optimism for the franchise moving forward.

entries.title: Is your home budget around $500,000? Three options to consider in D.C, Maryland and Virginia
entries.summary: Our weekly column compares home listings across the DMV.
entries.content:
For many first-time homebuyers in the DMV, it’s the price that drives everything, rather than a particular home style or neighborhood. Depending on where they work or where they want their kids to attend school, they may be willing to look at homes in D.C., Maryland and Virginia as long as the price is right.

Buying a home priced at $500,000, which is below what Bright MLS says is the median sales price of $610,000 in the D.C. region, requires a minimum income of about $150,000 to $160,000. However, you need to talk to a lender who can help you estimate how much you can borrow based on your other debt, the size of your down payment and associated costs such as a homeowner or condo association fee, in addition to taxes and insurance. We found two townhouses and a condo priced between $499,000 and $600,000 to consider.

Which would you choose? Or, have a comparison you’d like to see in an upcoming column? Let us know at metro@washingtonsun.com.

D.C.

The price: $565,000

The specifics: This 960-square-foot townhouse, built in 1900 and renovated in 2022 and 2025, has two bedrooms and 1.5 bathrooms.

The vibe: Updated city living.

What makes it special: While this rowhouse is a bit above $500,000, it doesn’t have an HOA fee that would increase your monthly costs. Located in the Kingman Park neighborhood not far from H Street Northeast, the two-level townhouse has a fireplace flanked by built-in bookcases in the living room, French doors leading to a fully fenced yard with a deck, an updated kitchen, a powder room and a separate dining room. The two bedrooms are upstairs, along with a renovated full bathroom, a stacked washer and dryer and multiple closets. The roof was resealed and a skylight installed in 2025, while the heating, air conditioning and water heater were upgraded in 2022.

Maryland

The specifics: This 1,868-square-foot townhouse, built in 2011, has three bedrooms and 2.5 bathrooms. Monthly HOA and condo/co-op fees: $378

The vibe: Amenity-rich community.

What makes it special: Located in the Parklands at Watkins Mill, walkable to a MARC train station and shops, this community has a pool, tennis, playgrounds and a gym. It’s also a short drive to the Kentlands and Downtown Crown for more shops and restaurants. The main level of the house has an open floor plan kitchen, living area and dining area, hardwood floors, big windows, a powder room and access to the one-car garage. Upstairs, the primary suite has two walk-in closets and a private bathroom, plus there are two additional bedrooms (one with a balcony), another full bathroom and a laundry room.

Agent: Meaghan Miller, TTR Sotheby’s International Realty

Virginia

UntitledThe listing: 1570 Spring Gate Drive, Unit 7408, McLean

The price: $499,000

The specifics: This two-bedroom, two-bathroom condo, which includes a garage parking space, was built in 1997. It’s the largest floor plan at the Gates of McLean, with 1,169 square feet. Monthly condo fee: $720.

The vibe: Walkable condo with amenities.

What makes it special: This top-floor unit in an elevator building has a balcony accessible from the living room and one of the bedrooms, and a gas fireplace. The floor plan includes a separate kitchen with an adjacent laundry room, and an open living and dining room with bedrooms on either side for privacy. The primary suite has a walk-in closet, a second closet and a private full bathroom. The kitchen and bathrooms have been renovated. Community amenities include a pool, clubhouse, fitness center, business center and playgrounds. Shops and the McLean Metro station are within 10 minutes’ walk.

entries.title: The Washington Sun Metro: On Edge
entries.content:
Good morning. This is The Washington Sun Metro Newsletter for Oct. 27, 2026. You can get it in your inbox every day by signing up here — it’s free!

In today’s newsletter: Early voting, evictions and the big questions facing Jayden Daniels. 

Capital Weather’s Daily Digit — 9/10. A perpetual parade of autumn perfection persists through the end of October. All treats, no tricks! Read the full forecast.





THE LATEST


“NATL GUARD STAY AWAY” 

That was the message chalked onto the sidewalk near a polling place in Columbia Heights on Monday morning, when a weeklong period of in-person early voting kicked off.

D.C. may not be particularly politically competitive or important in this year’s midterm elections, but The Washington Sun’s Martin Austermuhle reports that some activists and residents remain nervous about the possibility that federal agents or the National Guard may show up at or near polling places — potentially intimidating voters.

Fears of such intimidation spiked this month when Guard troops were spotted standing by a ballot drop box in Foggy Bottom. That prompted the D.C. Board of Elections to formally ask Guard leadership to ensure it wouldn’t happen again; the leadership quickly responded to say that troops “are directed not to monitor or secure polling locations.”

After the incident, D.C. Attorney General Brian Schwalb issued guidance to election officials and residents confirming that federal law bans troops from operating near polling places, and prohibits anyone from intimidating or coercing voters or interfering with the work of a local election official. The elections board also told all volunteer coordinators of D.C. polling places that the National Guard, ICE and any other federal agents have to stay at least 50 feet away.

The general uneasiness comes as the Trump administration has ramped up election-related efforts, including an unsuccessful push to rein in the use of mail ballots and more recent litigation taking aim at alleged voting by noncitizens. The latter fight hits close to home in D.C., where noncitizens are legally allowed to cast ballots for local offices, but not federal ones.

Early in-person voting will continue in D.C. through Sunday; all the locations can be found here. Voters can also leave their ballot at any of the 55 drop boxes around D.C. As of Monday morning, more than 20,000 voters had opted for a drop box.





DEEP DIVE

Evictions are at a record high in D.C. right now, and as those cases crawl through the backlogged court system, tenants build up insurmountable arrears while housing providers go without income. Landlords say it’s an economic “death spiral.”

The D.C. Council is floating a pilot program that would help avoid the eviction process altogether. The bill, dubbed the “SHARE Act,” would require tenants who owe less than three months or $6,000 in unpaid rent to enter mediation with their landlord to talk things out before a case gets filed.

What then? A tenant can agree to move out, get repairs to their unit or, in some cases, get a third of their debt cleared by the District and another third forgiven by the landlord — if they cover the remaining balance.

“We support voluntary mediation coupled with rental assistance, and this is a good pilot,” Dean Hunter, the CEO of D.C.’s Small Multifamily Owners Association, told The Sun. Hunter added that he believes the pilot should begin sooner than fiscal year 2028 to relieve the current rent payment “crisis.”

At a public hearing yesterday, the D.C. attorney general’s office testified that it supports the idea, and wants to see the pilot strengthened by including legal representation for tenants and handling 5,000 cases instead of the proposed 2,000. An executive at real estate firm WC Smith said he wants it canned, over worries that it’ll encourage residents to build up debts, knowing two-thirds might be covered for them.

At-large council member Robert White, who introduced the bill, said the test could model a way to keep landlords, tenants and courts afloat.

“We cannot evict our way out of the rental arrears crisis,” he said.





FROM THE DISTRICT

A man was fatally stabbed at the D.C. Jail on Sunday with a “makeshift weapon,” The Sun’s Jenny Gathright reports. He’s the fourth person to die while in D.C. Department of Corrections custody this year.

The VA requested an emergency order of kitchen equipment for its D.C. medical center after a June accreditation survey found insect debris and unidentified residue in one of the facility’s kitchens, The Sun’s Yasmeen Khan reports. According to the contracting request for the items, continuing to work with the kitchen’s equipment posed an “ongoing infection control risk.”

Stilettos in the Fast Lane: The District is hosting its 39th annual 17th Street High Heel Race tonight. The event celebrates the District’s LGBTQIA+ community with costumes, live music and local drag performers.

The race is one of D.C.’s most “visually stunning” events, said Japer Bowles, executive director of the mayor’s office of LGBTQ affairs. The Sun’s Justice Covert reports that more than 250 people are expected to compete in the mad dash from R Street to Church Street at 9 p.m.

“Some say it’s a really, really quick race, you know, 45 seconds for some to get from one block to the end,” Bowles said. “But, for a lot, they take it all in and they do the full strut in a costume.”

Bowles said the winner will receive a gift basket worth more than $200 in gift cards and discounts from businesses along 17th Street. He offered that the best strategy is to “wear boots.”





FROM VIRGINIA

A Manassas Park High School teacher is facing charges of illegally possessing a firearm on school property after a loaded handgun was found on the ground across the street in the parking lot of Manassas Park Middle School early Monday, Covert reports.

School officials said on social media they closed all schools in the area “out of an abundance of caution” to give the police department time to investigate. A later update noted that the staff member was placed on leave per school policy.

A lawsuit filed by the family of a Northern Virginia man who died in Alexandria police custody in August 2025 alleges that the two officers who arrested him “acted with reckless disregard” for his safety, and that the city did not properly train officers on how to respond to detainees who need medical attention, The Sun’s Kendall Staton reports.

The man accused of beheading the Iwo Jima memorial statue in Quantico was granted bond on Monday, ABC7 reports, though ICE has issued him a detainer.





WHAT YOU GET FOR $500,000

This week’s real estate column looks at what buyers can get for around $500,000 in the D.C. area.

Where is this house listed? Click on your guess to see the answer:

  1. Maryland
  2. Virginia
  3. D.C.




SPORTS

How good has Jayden Daniels been this year? Well, the answer is complicated. The third-year quarterback has had his ups and downs this season as Washington has stumbled through a 1-4-1 start. Dan Pizzuta takes a deeper look at the numbers to answer three big questions: Has Daniels been effective under center? Why has he struggled under pressure? And how can he overcome the loss of receiver Terry McLaurin?

Speaking of consistency, The Sun’s Martenzie Johnson reports that coach Dan Quinn believes it is Washington’s biggest issue.

“My belief in them as a group is really strong,” Quinn said Monday at his weekly press conference. “We’ve been in every game and just, I haven’t loved all four quarters together. That’s what we’re chasing.”

The team will be closer to full strength coming out of the bye, with quarterback Marcus Mariota and defensive lineman Charles Omenihu set to return to practice this week.

Mystics center Shakira Austin earned All-WNBA second team honors after a career season. The DMV native averaged 17 points and 9.5 rebounds, serving as a veteran leader on a Mystics team that surpassed expectations. The Sun’s Alex Schiffer reports that Austin is the first Mystics player since 2021 to earn a spot on an all-league team.



Thank you for reading! If you liked this newsletter, please forward it to a friend. If someone shared it with you, please sign up — it’s free! Got a tip or comments to share? Email us at metro@washsun.com. Finally, the answer to yesterday’s trivia question was A) Fort Totten. It was never considered as a D.C. United stadium site. A special shout-out to Candace Butler, who answered first.

The newsletter was produced by Andrew Burton, Michael Errigo and Nikie Johnson.

entries.title: Morning Sun: One Week
entries.content:
Today’s notice: The latest from the last week of the midterms. Plus: Out of the blue, we thought we’d look into political spending at The Cheesecake Factory. And: What more strikes on Iran would mean.

The Washington Sun has a new newsletter starting Nov. 9: Congressional reporters Igor Bobic and Oriana González are taking you inside the Capitol in The Stakeout. Sign up now.





THE MAP


Choose your own adventure, one week out: If Republicans keep control of the House after next week’s midterms, it would objectively be very surprising. Every major prognosticator pegs Democrats’ chances to take the House at around 90% or higher.

The Senate, however … No one can agree on anything other than Democrats have a possibility of success. “Nate” Silver Bulletin’s FLIPR says Dems have a 76% chance of winning, while The Economist puts their chances at 56%. (Other forecasters generally fall somewhere in the middle of those two.) The national fight is for the Senate, and it is down to the wire.

Mississippi: Presidential voter fraud bounty. Before he took the stage to shore up Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith, who is in a shockingly competitive race, Donald Trump offered $1 million to anyone who can provide information that leads to “the arrest and conviction” of election fraudsters. The president posted the reward to Truth Social.

Texas: Does James Talarico have a problem? Some strategists and local lawmakers think Talarico is falling short with Black voters — criticism that hasplagued him since the primary — and that an enthusiasm gap could make the difference on whether he is able to beat Republican Ken Paxton, The Sun’s Kadia Goba, Daniella Diaz and Marissa Martinez report.

New York: Mike Lawler works the drive-thru. Emulating Trump in 2024, the Republican congressman from the state’s 17th District served customers at McDonald’s yesterday. Lawler used the stunt to talk up the legislative win he hopes propels him to reelection: “The extra SALT is in the bag,” he told customers as he handed them their orders.

Iowa: Josh Turek says he’s running Trump’s playbook. MAGA “accurately identified that the status quo was not working for the average person,” the Democratic Senate nominee told The Sun’s Elena Schneider at a campaign stop in Cedar Rapids yesterday. Turek suggested his closing argument comes down to understanding why voters chose Trump and channeling their frustrations over prices: “Everything that he has done has driven it the opposite direction.”

Ohio: Jim Jordan sidesteps Vivek’s ad. The congressman and potential GOP conference leadership candidate didn’t join other Ohio Republicans in condemning the visceral ad from the party’s gubernatorial nominee. “I think this is the Democrats wanting to deflect from Amy Acton’s record,” Jordan told The Sun’s Reese Gorman at a campaign stop in South Carolina yesterday. “Remember, she’s been called the Fauci of Ohio.”

South Carolina: Paging Ralph Norman. Reese also talked to Republican Rep. Russell Fry of the 7th Congressional District out on the trail for Sen. Darline Graham. Fry called out Norman, who has said he won’t campaign for Graham. Both men ran against Graham in the primary. “He didn’t win. I didn’t win, either,” Fry told Reese. “I hope that he does, in the final eight days, step into the, you know, step into the sunlight a little bit and help his Republican nominee.”

Wisconsin: Kamala Harris is back on the trail. The former vice president hit Milwaukee to deliver a nine-minute speech to an excited but half-full room at a women-focused event to boost the gubernatorial ambitions of Democratic nominee David Crowley. The Sun’s Jasmine Wright was there. Trump was on everyone’s mind. “You warned us,” one attendee shouted to Harris.

Kansas: Exclusive polling hypes Democrats’ chances. The Senate race is where the attention is, but new internal polling shared with The Sun shows there may be more to watch in the state. A survey conducted for the Democratic Attorneys General Association finds Democratic AG nominee Chris Mann leading Republican incumbent Kris Kobach, 48-44.

Minnesota: The same polling shows Democrats’ challenges. The DAGA polling found incumbent Democratic AG Keith Ellison tied with Republican nominee Ron Schutz, 48-48. The pollster says “remaining soft supporters and undecided voters tilt heavily Democratic by self-identification.” It’s another sign that Democrats are seeing tough sledding in this blue state. Read the entire DAGA memo, which includes fresh numbers from across the country.

North Carolina: Air war resumes. Republican Senate nominee Michael Whatley went back on the air yesterday after pulling his ads a couple weeks ago when national money fled the race amid sinking poll numbers. Democrat Roy Cooper’s campaign announced a new buy, too — a seven-figure purchase that’s larger than the amount of money Whatley’s campaign has on hand, The Sun’s Chase Pellegrini de Paur notes.

FROM THE CHEESECAKE FACTORY


Meet the pols who spent the most money on events at The Cheesecake Factory since 2015, per FEC reports scrutinized by The Sun’s Dave Levinthal. First is the RNC, with around $7,800. Then comes Sen. Tim Scott (R-South Carolina), who racked up $4,900 there between his Senate campaigns and failed presidential bid. Top Democrats include EMILYs List at around $1,100 and Reps. Wesley Bell (D-Missouri) and Ted Lieu (D-California) at less than $1,000. The campaign of Sen. John Fetterman (D-Pennsylvania) spent around $358. Trump’s campaign spent a whopping $132.38 there; Joe Biden’s campaign, nada.

These figures, from Republicans anyway, might shoot up soon thanks to the ongoing fixation with The Cheesecake Factory since Barack Obama namechecked it while insulting Trump’s taste in White House gilding the other night. The Sun’s Manuela Silva and Andrew Van Dam look at the rhetoric and the facts around this fancy mall eatery. Home values in ZIP codes within 3 miles of a Cheesecake Factory are about 27% higher than comparable areas without one, they write.

What more U.S. strikes on Iran would mean: Former U.S. officials and experts question whether another round of strikes like the president is reportedly considering could deliver the Trump administration’s elusive strategic victory in Iran, The Sun’s Joe Gould reports. “I fail to see how the United States and Israel are three or four days of strikes away from what would be a strategic-level change,” former Pentagon official Jason Campbell told Joe.

entries.title: Super PACs Are Supposed to Be Transparent. They’re Still Awash in ‘Dark Money.’
entries.summary: Groups tied to both Democratic and Republican leaders are regularly using a legal provision that lets them hide root funding sources.
entries.content:
Super PACs closely aligned with Democratic and Republican congressional leaders have disclosed record donations from affiliated “dark money” groups, obscuring the source of hundreds of millions of dollars influencing House and Senate midterm elections next week.

This torrent of secret money exploits a provision in federal election law that allows super PACs, which must publicly disclose the identities of their contributors, to accept donations from certain nonprofits, trade groups, unions and shell corporations, which themselves are generally exempt.

Dark money groups have for years given tens of millions of dollars to Republican super PACs Senate Leadership Fund and Congressional Leadership Fund and Democratic super PACs Senate Majority PAC and House Majority PAC.

But this election cycle, these dark money affiliates have collectively donated more than $392 million to the four leadership-aligned super PACs as of Oct. 14, according to a Washington Sun analysis of Federal Election Commission data.

That’s more than double the $181.9 million these super PACs reported receiving through the same period in the 2024 election cycle, a previous record.
https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/WgDr8/5/Not only are these four super PACs receiving more total donations from their dark money affiliates than in any previous election cycle, but those dark donations make up a greater percentage of the super PACs’ overall fundraising than ever before, according to The Sun’s analysis.

Super PACs are “super” because they are legally allowed to raise and spend unlimited amounts of money to advocate for and against political candidates, although they cannot directly donate money to candidates’ own campaigns. They’re also restricted in how they may coordinate their efforts with candidate committees.

The congressional leadership-aligned super PACs are currently four of the five largest outside spenders this election cycle, according to OpenSecrets, a nonpartisan nonprofit that tracks the flow of money in American politics.

Republicans’ Senate Leadership Fund is chief among them, having received more than $132.9 million from the dark money nonprofit group One Nation as of Oct. 14, according to FEC data.

That’s a 148% increase from the $53.6 million One Nation steered into the Senate Leadership Fund during the 2024 election cycle. Before that, the most money that the Senate Leadership Fund reported receiving from One Nation through the same period was $62.6 million during the 2020 election cycle.

While One Nation and the Senate Leadership Fund are technically separate entities, their logos hung side by side in the entryway of a Washington office that The Sun visited in November.

And Republicans’ Congressional Leadership Fund disclosed sending its affiliated dark money group, American Action Network, $329,670 as “reimbursement for shared labor, rent, utilities,” according to its latest report to the FEC, indicating some shared operations.

The Congressional Leadership Fund reported receiving around $64 million from American Action Network so far this election cycle, according to FEC data, a nearly 60% surge from $40 million at the same point during the 2024 cycle.

The Senate Leadership Fund and Congressional Leadership Fund did not respond to requests for comment.

On the left, the total amount of dark money flowing into Democratic super PACs Senate Majority PAC and House Majority PAC has more than doubled from the 2024 election cycle, according to FEC data.

As of Oct. 14, Senate Majority PAC has reported receiving $102 million from its affiliated dark money group, Majority Forward. That’s up from about $45 million through the same period during the 2024 election cycle and $48 million during the 2022 election cycle.

Around 29% of the money that the Senate Majority PAC has raised through the same period has come from Majority Forward — up from 14% through the same period in 2024, 19% in 2022 and 3% in 2020.

And House Majority PAC has reported receiving $93.7 million from House Majority Forward, up from $42.5 million during the 2024 election cycle and $7 million during the 2022 election cycle.

House Majority Forward accounted for 32% of all the money House Majority PAC has raised as of Oct. 14. That’s up from 19% of all fundraising through the same point in the 2024 election cycle and 5% through the same period in both the 2022 and 2020 election cycles, according to The Sun’s analysis of FEC data.

House Majority PAC declined to comment. The Senate Majority PAC did not respond to requests for comment.

Some congressional Democrats have pushed — unsuccessfully — for legislation that would require greater disclosure of dark money donations.

But the Democrats’ two congressional leadership-aligned super PACs have nevertheless invited donations through their dark money groups more and more over the last few election cycles.

“While Democrats in Congress continue to push for reforms to bring more transparency to political spending to end dark money, there's a lot of Democratic operatives out there who say the party needs to fight fire with fire, and there are politicians who've been willing to embrace that,” Michael Beckel, money in politics reform director at Issue One, told The Sun.

The Republican-aligned super PACs are also bringing in a greater percentage of their overall fundraising from affiliated dark money groups than they have in previous election cycles, although both super PACs embraced these donations a bit earlier than their Democratic counterparts.

One Nation made up more than 24% of all donations to the Senate Leadership Fund as of Oct. 14, according to FEC data. That’s up from 19% through the same period in 2024, 21% in 2022 and 20% in 2020.

Around 25% of the Congressional Leadership Fund’s fundraising as of Oct. 14 came from American Action Network — up from 17% through the same period in 2024, 19% in 2022 and 18% in 2020.

Beyond the four congressional leadership super PACs, many other super PACs follow a similar playbook: More than $1 billion in dark money had already poured in the 2026 midterms by the end of August, when The New York Times published an analysis that included political advertising data and tax filings in addition to campaign finance disclosures.

Few of the House and Senate races that will determine control of Congress are untouched by dark money, which is sometimes passed through multiple nonprofits and political groups before getting spent in the form of political attack ads or mailers.

Take, for instance, the U.S. Senate race in Michigan. Undisclosed donors gave money to the nonprofit Right Vote, which then gave to conservative super PAC Sentinel Action Fund, which in turn spent more than $1.6 million against Democrat Abdul El-Sayed across 12 expenditures.

Undisclosed donors also gave an undisclosed amount of money to Senate Opportunity Fund, a nonprofit that doesn't disclose its donors, which gave to High Plains PAC, which spent $258,000 against El-Sayed across three payments.

Meanwhile, mystery donors gave to Majority Forward and the Economic Opportunity Fund, which gave to the Senate Majority PAC, which then gave to pro-Democratic super PAC WinSenate, which spent over $9 million against the Republican nominee in Michigan, former Rep. Mike Rogers.
Rogers.ElSayed (2829x1886, AR: 1.50)El-Sayed has also benefited from a trail of dark money to the Senate Majority PAC, which in turn gave to WinSenate, which spent in support of the Democrat. Right Vote gave $5 million to the Sentinel Action Fund, which spent $1.45 million total in support of Rogers.

In Maine, dark money is being spent to support and oppose Republican Sen. Susan Collins and her democratic challenger, Troy Jackson. Sentinel Action Fund sent $1.5 million to the Lead Maine Committee, which has spent around $370,000 supporting Collins. WinSenate has spent nearly $4.5 million in support of Jackson.

“The amount of money that are being pumped into elections this cycle is just off the charts compared to previous years, and I think a lot of voters all across the political spectrum are looking for politicians to actually de-escalate the political fundraising arms race,” Beckel told The Sun.

Voters across the political spectrum generally believe there is too much money in politics, a frustration some Republican and Democratic candidates have been leaning into this election cycle.

But to date, Democrats and Republicans have been unwilling to coalesce around bipartisan reforms to change the way national elections are funded. The Supreme Court, for its part, has made it easier this election cycle for party committees to spend unlimited sums in coordination with candidates — and access lower television and radio advertising prices, which are not available to super PACs.

entries.title: As Early Voting Begins in D.C., Some Prepare for Federal Interference
entries.summary: “Voter intimidation can take many forms,” says one activist.
entries.content:
Candidates and campaigners in D.C. know well that they can’t get within 50 feet of polling places. But a message chalked onto the sidewalk outside an early-voting center in Columbia Heights on Monday extended that reminder to another group: “NATL GUARD STAY AWAY.”

A weeklong period of in-person early voting kicked off in D.C. on Monday amidst heightened national political tension and local concerns over possible federal interference — including by federal agents or National Guard troops appearing near or around polling places.

Those worries spiked earlier this month when guard members were seen standing next to a ballot drop box in Foggy Bottom, prompting the D.C. Board of Elections to formally request they stop doing so because it could intimidate voters. National Guard leadership quickly responded, saying that troops in D.C. “are directed not to monitor or secure polling locations.”

“It doesn’t seem like there is an active threat, but of course we’ve seen the way that federal agents and the Guard have flouted authority in the past and we should be prepared to make sure voters feel safe this election,” said Aparna Raj, the Democratic nominee for the Ward 1 seat on the D.C. Council.

Sign up for The Washington Sun Metro newsletter for essential coverage of the D.C. region.

Those preparations have taken various forms in recent weeks. D.C. Attorney General Brian Schwalb’s office issued guidance to residents and election officials outlining what federal agents and troops can and can’t do regarding the city’s upcoming election. In short, they’re legally restricted from doing much of anything.

“An array of federal statutes bars federal employees, law enforcement, and the military from using their official power to interfere with an election,” read the guidance. “Federal law generally prohibits the federal government from sending the military or ‘armed men,’ including federal law-enforcement officers or National Guard troops, to a polling place. Federal law also forbids anyone from intimidating or coercing voters in federal elections and from interfering with an election officer’s discharge of their duties.”

The elections board has worked that guidance into its training for volunteer coordinators of the city’s polling places.

“In all site coordinator training classes, [they] were instructed that the National Guard, ICE and similar organizations are not allowed in the vote centers or within the 50-foot electioneering area unless they are there to vote,” said Sarah Graham, a spokesperson for the board. “And If they appear and there is any perception of voter intimidation, they should contact our general counsel's office or call 911.”

A number of groups, including Free D.C., Harriet’s Wildest Dreams, the Lawyers' Committee for Civil Rights Under Law and Common Cause, will have independent observers at polling places “who can document any problems that arise, and it’s not just law enforcement or soldiers — it’s any irregularities,” said Alex Dodds, a campaign director with Free D.C.

The groups hosted a training session on Monday night, where organizers walked more than 120 volunteers through a series of voting-related scenarios, what D.C. law says and how they should respond.

“Voter intimidation can take many forms,” said Joe DeMartin of the Advancement Project. “Law-enforcement presence, yes. Soldiers hanging out by the polls. ICE officers.”

The general uneasiness comes as the Trump administration has ramped up election-related efforts leading up to the midterms, including an unsuccessful push to rein in the use of mail ballots and more recent litigation taking aim at alleged voting by noncitizens.

While D.C. doesn’t factor into the broader national fight over which party will ultimately control Congress — it lacks voting representation, after all — Lauren Bonds of the National Police Accountability Project said there’s still reason to be concerned about possible electoral interference or intimidation by federal agents or the National Guard.

“D.C. has been a test ground for what federal law enforcement and the National Guard can get away with,” she said. “It could result in federal law enforcement showing up in places where elections are closer or more consequential. This administration is using D.C. to see what they can get away with.”

Bonds added that even if the city’s elections aren’t nationally consequential, D.C. voters could be dissuaded from voting if the National Guard or federal agents are present at or around polling places. That could impact noncitizen D.C. residents, who are legally allowed to vote in local elections (but are still barred from voting in federal races).

“People should care if people are being deterred from voting because of law enforcement,” she said.

More broadly, Dodds argued that even if D.C. won’t help decide who controls Congress, there are still legitimate reasons to fear the federal government could try to interfere in the city’s local elections.

“We’ve heard Trump threaten our mayoral candidate from the Oval Office,” she said. “Anyone who doesn’t think D.C. isn’t important for Trump is missing the bigger picture about how authoritarian leaders try to stay in power.”

entries.title: All-DMV High School Volleyball Players of Week 9
entries.summary: This week’s group includes record-breakers from Richard Montgomery and Flint Hill.
entries.content:
This story is part of The Washington Sun’s All-DMV coverage. All-DMV is a new collaboration between The Sun, Fox 5 DC, NBC4 Washington and WTOP News, aimed at covering the D.C. area’s best high school athletes. You can find past players of the week and more information about All-DMV here.

With the volleyball regular season nearing completion, here’s who closed October out strong to earn All-DMV Player of the Week:

Ana Djordjevic, Senior, Libero, Richard Montgomery

Richard Montgomery’s all-time leader in digs, Djordjevic has been the steady defensive presence that the Rockets have leaned on through another dominant fall campaign. The senior helped lead her team to dominant sweeps over Wootton and Bethesda-Chevy Chase last week, her command of the back line allowing the team’s efficient offense to thrive. Djordjevic eclipsed 600 career digs with an 11-dig performance against the Barons on Friday, bringing her season tally to 163.

“Her ownership of the back line really makes it run like a well-oiled machine,” coach Gretchen Barber-Strunk said. “Ana is a key component to making the team flow and work together.”

Djordjevic has also made her mark at the service line for Barber-Strunk’s team. The Rockets’ libero is serving with 92% accuracy and has accumulated 32 service aces this year, including five against Wootton last week.

Hunter Ross, Senior, Outside Hitter, Flint Hill

If you had asked Flint Hill coach Thai Nguyen four years ago whether Ross was capable of becoming the Huskies’ all-time leader in kills, his answer would have been simple.

“Heck no!” Nguyen said. “When she came in as a freshman, skinny little kid, hardly any body control, goofy as heck … if you would have told me she was going to break it, I would have said ‘No way.’”

Ross broke the record last week against Colgan. The UCLA commit needed three kills to become Flint Hill’s all-time leader, and she finished with 27 putaways and nine service aces in a four-set victory.

Flint Hill, which has produced a bevy of Division I volleyball talent in recent years, has leaned on Ross to continue the program’s rich winning tradition. She’s turned her offense up a notch with the playoffs around the corner — Friday’s record-breaking performance was Ross’ fourth straight match with at least 20 kills.

“It’s all her dedication, her hard work, putting in many hours of training and fine-tuning her craft,” Nguyen said. “She did it on her own.”

Nyah Tucker, Senior, Outside Hitter, Oxon Hill

Tucker is the only four-year starter on an Oxon Hill team looking to make a playoff push in Prince George’s County. With many new players slotting into fresh roles this year, coach Andria Bynum has relied heavily on her senior outside hitter.

Tucker has shown up for the Clippers in efficient fashion. She is hitting at a hyper-efficient .465 clip for a team that hasn’t lost since September. With the playoffs right around the corner, Tucker is averaging over two kills per set and has also racked up 81 service aces on the season.

“[Her teammates] call her the big dog,” Bynum said. “It’s been a lot of pressure on her … but she’s really responded well to being that lone senior leader.”

entries.title: Texas Democrats Are Frustrated Talarico Hasn't Done More to Win Black Voters
entries.summary: “The question is how many Black people are going to show up to vote," said one Texas Democrat.
entries.content:
A $25 million Black voter outreach initiative. An interview on “The Breakfast Club.” Hosting a fundraiser at Texas Southern University, an HBCU in Houston.

Texas state Rep. James Talarico is attempting to gain ground with Texas’ 2.7 million Black voters as he seeks to become the first Democrat elected statewide in Texas in more than three decades.

But some strategists and local lawmakers think Talarico is falling short — criticism that has plagued him since the primary — and that an enthusiasm gap from Black voters could make the difference on whether he is able to beat state Attorney General Ken Paxton, the Republican candidate, next week.

“What I'm seeing with what is spent doesn't look or feel anything like $25 million at all. … He really does need to give more, he really does,” said Democratic state Rep. Jolanda Jones, who serves in a predominantly Black district in Houston and endorsed Talarico.

Polling has found Talarico leading Paxton among Black voters — but some Democrats are worried that not enough enthusiasm from Black voters will eat into any overall margin Talarico might have.

“The question is not whether Talarico gets the majority of the Black vote because Talarico is going to get the majority of Black votes,” Jones said. “The question is how many Black people are going to show up to vote.”

How enthusiastic Black voters are for Talarico won’t be clear until after Election Day.

But some surrogates are already criticizing the state representative’s investment in shoring up his support among Black voters as too late.

“Where he deserves credit is that he did with Latino voters what we've been asking the Democratic Party to do with Black voters. He went in early, Day 1. He started engaging Latino voters. He built in infrastructure within his campaign run by Latinos to develop strategy to engage Latinos,” Ashley Etienne, a former Democratic White House and congressional aide, told The Washington Sun.

But Etienne thinks that the campaign should be trying harder to make similar gains among Black Texans.

Traci Gibson, the first Black chair of the Harris County Democratic Party, said she has been visiting barber shops across the county to talk to Black men, most of whom she said did not recognize Talarico’s name.

"I think he's done a few things, maybe once a month in Harris County,” Gibson said. “I would think that the largest county in Texas would get more touch points with Black voters, so I think there is room for additional pushes.”

In a statement, the Talarico campaign highlighted his Black voter outreach efforts.

“Texas deserves a senator that will fight for Black Texans,” said JT Ennis, a spokesperson for the Talarico campaign. “It’s why James stands up to racist redistricting maps, champions HBCU funding, and supports programs that invest in Black owned businesses, increase access to capital, and provide home ownership grants to Black communities.”

In response to Jones specifically, the Talarico campaign pointed The Sun to an interview she gave local media earlier this month, in which she reiterated her endorsement for Talarico and said she was pleased with his announced investment. The Sun’s interview with her took place several days later.

Perhaps the clearest sign that Talarico may be falling short with Black voters is the lack of a public campaign presence from U.S. Rep. Jasmine Crockett, a popular Black Democrat who lost the Senate primary to Talarico. Black voters overwhelmingly backed her in that contest, and she has since endorsed him.

But she has been noticeably absent from his events, which has led to criticism from some observers who believe she should join him in key neighborhoods on the trail.

CNN anchor Laura Coates pressed Crockett on her show in August about why she wouldn’t campaign with Talarico — Crockett dodged the question repeatedly.

Crockett has pushed back against criticism related to her absence on the campaign, arguing Talarico is focused on flipping Republicans angry over the economy rather than courting Black voters.

“We had two completely different philosophies,” Crockett told The Sun, noting that other national Black surrogates like former Vice President Kamala Harris and Sen. Rafael Warnock (D-Georgia) have yet to campaign with Talarico. “His philosophy wasn't, ‘We’ve got enough Democrats. We just got to turn out these disaffected kind of folks that nobody ever talks to.’ His philosophy was: ‘I’m going to go get Republicans.’”

During an interview with The Grio this summer, Talarico extended an open invitation to Crockett to campaign with him. She told The Sun that she rejected an invitation to speak at a convention and that he has otherwise not directly asked her to join him on the campaign trail.

“I go where I'm asked to be,” she said. “We have not been asked.”

The Talarico campaign did not comment when asked if it had invited the lawmaker to join him.

Many Democrats believe her popularity with the base could help Talarico win over the crucial voting bloc.

“She has become a really trusted messenger with Black voters,” said Brianna Brown, executive director of the Texas Organizing Project, whose PAC endorsed Crockett in the primary. “I think that it could help credentialize Talarico in the community that don't know him, that do know Jasmine.”

But the primary was so contentious that the relationship between Crockett and Talarico grew uneasy and things didn’t improve much afterwards — some Crockett supporters bashed Talarico for not doing enough to support Black communities in Texas and voiced frustration over their candidate's loss.

Democratic state Rep. Ron Reynolds, a Black lawmaker who endorsed Crockett in the primary but backed Talarico after he won the nomination, said he faced some of the residual anger that bubbled among disappointed Crockett voters afterward. A month after the primary, he said he and Talarico were dining at a soul food restaurant in Houston’s Third Ward when some voters came up to Reynolds to lambast him for supporting a white man, calling him a “sellout.”

Those sentiments have since calmed down, the state representative said, particularly because Talarico has taken all the criticism on the chin to run an “almost flawless campaign.”

“There were some environments where people were … very much pro-Crockett, and they had animus towards his campaign, like, ‘We should skip the race, we should undervote,’” Reynolds said. “I think he's come a long way on the heels of that primary to win over African American voters.”

Others also praise the outreach Talarico has done to connect with Black voters.

"He’s a phenomenal candidate, as was Jasmine. I was running my own race in the primary, so I wasn’t involved in any other races," Rep. Christian Menefee, a Black Democrat from Texas, told The Sun over text. "I told both senate candidates during the primary that as soon as my primary was over, I was going to be all in for the Dem Nominee in the general. I spoke with James the day after the primary to get going.”

“Talarico has been at the church, the club, and everywhere in between."

entries.title: As the Number of Days Until the Election Falls, Trump’s Numbers Keep Growing
entries.summary: A political rhetoric expert says it’s “truthful hyperbole,” while an economist says that even the president’s truthful claims often lack the necessary context.
entries.content:
How much money has been invested in the United States during President Donald Trump’s second term? According to Trump at recent events, that number is $21 trillion. It’s also been $22 trillion. And $22.2 trillion.

In the run-up to next week’s midterm elections, Trump has hit the road, and the numbers he’s bragging about in his stump speech have grown. Trump’s growing figures on investments, crowd size at his events and the health of the economy show a pattern, according to Ryan Skinnell, who teaches about political rhetoric at San Jose State University.

“He uses ‘truthful hyperbole,’” Skinnell said. “Making things bigger and grander and larger than they are. You can see it most often when there's some big event coming up, like an election, or he's anxious, nervous or scared about something.”

The growth in the top-line investment number — which the White House’s website reports is $11.3 trillion — hasn’t been limited to his recent campaign events. Trump said the number was $18 trillion in May, $19 trillion in July, $20 trillion in August and $21 trillion in September.

“The money that's being invested is $22.5 trillion,” Trump said Sunday at a Michigan campaign rally. “We have more growth than any country has ever had. We are doing better than any country has ever had.”

White House spokesperson Matthew Middleton deferred to Trump’s claims when asked about the difference between the president's statements and the White House website.

“President Trump is right,” Middleton said in a statement “This administration has secured many trillions of dollars in investments during his presidency.”

Economists say it’s hard to see how the investment total is rooted in reality.

“That’s a wild number with no basis in fact,” Josh Bivens, chief economist at the Economic Policy Institute, said in a statement to The Washington Sun. “The entire GDP of the U.S. is about $32 trillion, and business investment is around 14% of that.”

Angelo Carusone, the president of Media Matters — a nonprofit organization focused on misinformation analysis — said that conservative news outlets are reframing what the president says instead of parroting it as some outlets did during his first term and even earlier in this term. Trump, for instance, said more than 30,000 people showed up to his Oct. 14 rally in Kalispell, Montana. The venue's website says maximum occupancy is around 7,000.

Carusone said he hasn't seen Trump’s claim on the Montana crowd size repeated much by conservative media outlets. He said networks are already facing viewer pushback for defending Trump's economy and may want to avoid further isolating viewers by defending something “so obviously dumb and untrue.”

“They're not basically going crazy with the crowd size the way they had been in the past,” Carusone said, adding that he saw several outlets report the crowd size as being a few thousand people.

Near the end of his rally speeches, Trump often boasts of a robust economy, hitting on a similar set of talking points.

“Incomes for hardworking Americans have soared to the highest level ever recorded,” Trump said Oct. 19 at a Kansas rally. “More Americans are working today than at any time in the history of our country. And … the poverty rate has just reached its lowest level.”

While each of those facts is true, American University economics professor Kara Reynolds says Trump often omits the context that underlies why rising prices continue to top voters’ list of the most pressing issues facing the country.

Reynolds said rising incomes and stock market gains are highly skewed to the top earners.

“The stock market has been up a lot over the last two years. But the fact is that very few Americans actually own stock,” Reynolds said, noting the “typical, median voter” isn’t benefiting from those financial gains.

The rise in incomes and the stock market is also tied to the AI boom, which Reynolds said will benefit top earners even more.

“All of that AI growth is going to the top earners in society,” Reynolds continued. “The people that are going to be struggling more with inflation, the people who spend more of their money at the grocery store, the people who might be laid off under some of this AI structural transformation are in the lower income brackets.”

Reynolds said context is also missing from the unemployment and poverty rates Trump discusses; the unemployment rate does not count Americans who have stopped looking for work, and an alternative poverty measure called the Supplemental Poverty Rate paints a very different picture from Trump's claims.

“When you look at that poverty rate, it's virtually unchanged,” Reynolds said. “It's 13.1% now, compared to only 7.7% in 2021. It speaks to how much of a cut we've seen in government services and how that has kind of exacerbated poverty across the country.”

Skinnell said that Trump hasn’t seen much blowback from voters in past elections when he’s made similarly disputed claims.

“It seems like the things that he says should turn voters off,” Skinnell said, “But there's a very sophisticated sort of machine that washes out, or at least tries to wash out, the most extreme things he says.”

“It often,” Skinnell added, “works well enough to get him elected.”

entries.title: Three Big Questions for Jayden Daniels Coming Out of the Bye
entries.summary: It has been an up-and-down start for the Commanders’ third-year quarterback. We took a deeper look at the numbers.
entries.content:
The 2026 season was supposed to be a reset year for Jayden Daniels, after his incredible rookie year was followed by a mostly lost sophomore campaign. But the start to Year 3 has not been particularly smooth. Daniels missed two and a half games with a dislocated elbow that currently requires a brace. There have also been injuries across the offense, the latest being star wide receiver Terry McLaurin’s season-ending knee injury.

Still, we have enough game action to make an early evaluation of how Daniels is adjusting to the offense under new coordinator David Blough. Through Week 6, Daniels ranked 15th in the NFL in expected points added (EPA) per play and success rate, while he ranked 12th in ESPN’s QBR system — effectively measuring Daniels as a slightly-above-average quarterback through the first part of the season.

We took a closer look at how he has performed, with an eye towards what could be improved upon as the season unfolds.

Has He Been Effective Playing From Under Center?

This was one of the big talking points heading into the season. Part of the reason why Blough was hired as coordinator was to install an offense that could operate more frequently from under center, with the aim of opening up both the running and play-action games.

In the small sample we’ve seen from Daniels so far, the results haven’t been great. In shotgun, Daniels averages 0.12 EPA per play with a 44.5% success rate. When under center, he averages -0.22 EPA per play with a 40.9% success rate. Daniels only has 20 under-center dropbacks, but that’s also part of the issue. The lack of production there — and with Daniels clearly more comfortable playing out of shotgun — has stopped the offense from leaning into it more.

However, the run game improvement with Daniels on the field has been there. On 27 running back carries from under center with Daniels, the Commanders average 0.06 EPA per rush with a 48.1% success rate. From shotgun, the Commanders average -0.12 EPA per rush with a 31.6% success rate on 38 carries.

If Daniels can get more comfortable playing from under center during the second half of the season, the Commanders could see an uptick in their offensive performance.

Why Has He Struggled When Under Pressure?

Both the biggest improvement and decline from Daniels have to do with pressure. When Daniels hasn't been pressured this season, he’s been one of the best quarterbacks in the league statistically. His 0.55 EPA per play ranks second, only behind Lamar Jackson’s 0.72. He’s getting the ball out quickly (2.42 seconds to throw), and that has created open windows to throw. According to NFL Next Gen Stats, Daniels has the 12th-lowest rate of throws into a tight coverage window.

When not pressured, 53.9% of his throws have gone between 1-10 air yards. On a down-to-down basis, he’s been more willing than in previous seasons to take something underneath, get the completion and let his receivers try to run after the catch. In his first two seasons, just over 40% of Daniels’s passes went to that depth when not under pressure.

That isn’t to say Daniels has lacked risk-taking this season. When he’s gotten time to be clean in the pocket and rip it down the field, he’s made some nice throws. And his 3.5% completion percentage over expected is a career-high and 10th in the league.

The problems have come when he’s under pressure. Daniels ranks 28th in EPA per play under pressure, a far cry from his sixth-best ranking in 2024. Even though he has lowered his sack rate (7.9%) to a career low, his production has taken a dive when opposing pass rushes are able to throw him off schedule.

One reason? His throwaway rate (21.7%) when under pressure is the second-highest mark in the league. It’s possible that as he gets more comfortable in the offense, and in his return from injury, that his performance in this area could pick up. It’s difficult to believe a quarterback with Daniels’ athleticism would remain so poor under pressure.

How Can He Overcome the Loss of McLaurin?

One of the keys for Daniels heading into 2026 was reestablishing his connection with McLaurin. The duo was one of the league’s best in 2024, but never recaptured that magic in 2025. Now, with McLaurin out for the rest of the season, the Commanders will again be without their top quarterback and wide receiver on the field together.

The immediate answer should be more Antonio Williams. The third-round rookie has caught 10 of his 11 targets from Daniels for 145 yards. When paired with veteran Stefon Diggs, who has been the most-targeted receiver from Daniels and has been especially effective in the short-to-intermediate range, that’s not a bad 1-2 option. Adding either Treylon Burks or Dyami Brown to the two of them keeps an 11 personnel alignment (three receivers, one tight end, one running back) viable.

But the Commanders could also lean into heavier looks in 12 and 13 personnel to force defenses to play bigger. Over the past two weeks, Washington has sprinkled some of these plays in for big gains.

The ideal surroundings the Commanders may have wanted for Daniels haven’t played out, but the third-year quarterback is adapting and showing signs of the player who was one of the rising stars of the league as a rookie. Washington might not have the same team success in 2026 — although the NFC East remains wide open — but if Daniels takes a step forward in his development, there will be reason for optimism for the franchise moving forward.
