entries.title: Experts Warn Escalating Iran Strikes Could Bring Retaliation Rather Than a U.S. Victory
entries.summary: As Trump weighs fresh attacks, military analysts and former officials say the risks may outweigh the benefits.
entries.content:
President Donald Trump said he is weighing whether to strike Iran again or pursue a negotiated settlement, raising the prospect of a fresh American military campaign and questions about what another round of bombing could accomplish that months of intermittent fighting have not.

“Do I make a deal with them or do I finish them off? That’s the only question,” Trump said in a Sunday interview with Fox News, signaling he is still considering another major military operation.

The U.S. and Israeli militaries have reportedly developed plans for an intensive three-day bombing campaign against Iran, with an expanded target list that includes energy infrastructure and facilities vital to the Iranian economy. CNN reported that American forces could launch an operation within 96 hours of receiving Trump’s orders. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his team have openly advocated overthrowing Iran’s government.

But former U.S. officials and experts questioned whether another round of strikes could deliver the Trump administration’s elusive strategic victory. A successful campaign against Iran’s remaining missile forces, military installations or command infrastructure would not necessarily force its leaders to surrender or shatter the Islamic Republic’s security apparatus, told The Washington Sun.

And a broader campaign could expose U.S. troops and regional allies to retaliation, potentially pulling Washington into a more prolonged and destructive war.

Jason Campbell, a former Pentagon official now at the Middle East Institute, said U.S. military options appear confined to airstrikes, while Iran’s dispersed command structures have been designed to survive the destruction of military facilities and senior leaders.

“I fail to see how the United States and Israel are three or four days of strikes away from what would be a strategic-level change,” Campbell said.

Behnam Ben Taleblu, an Iran specialist at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies who has supported previous American military action against Iran, argued against new strikes. Trump has “a winning hand,” he said, by sticking with his naval blockade of the Strait of Hormuz and intensifying economic pressure.

“The president can box in Tehran more effectively and slow the Islamic Republic’s rebuild of its nuclear, missile and military programs, and drive the regime to have to expend a declining amount of capital on a greater series of things,” Taleblu said. “Rather than have Uncle Sam or Israel be blamed … you put the burden and the onus of escalation onto the regime.”

The Pentagon is preparing to reinforce its presence in the Middle East, with the 13th Marine Expeditionary Unit reportedly heading to the region, along with another aircraft carrier. Those deployments could add 10,000 to 15,000 sailors and Marines to the roughly 50,000 U.S. military personnel already in the region.

Military analysts said more ambitious objectives, including seizing Iranian territory or overthrowing the government, would require a major ground operation — far beyond the forces available in the region and what the administration has so far been willing to risk.

Analysts estimate that securing shipping through the Strait of Hormuz would require at least 100,000 troops to occupy hundreds of miles of Iranian coastline, extending some 30 miles inland to protect against Iranian missiles.

The operation would entail large-scale amphibious and airborne assaults along a marshy coastline with few suitable landing sites. American forces would have to assemble within range of Iranian missiles, then face conventional attacks and insurgent resistance once ashore, risking heavy casualties without a guaranteed result.

“Even if you wanted to do that, where on Earth in that region are you going to stage the sufficient forces to prepare for such an operation,” said Campbell, who recently war-gamed the scenario with military planners. “Because right now, Iran has either destroyed or made very unsafe pretty much every installation that the U.S. would potentially use for any kind of a major ground operation.”

Ben Connable, a former Marine officer and RAND Corporation military analyst now with the Battle Research Group, said another air campaign could weaken Iran’s conventional military without really changing the conflict. The U.S. hasn’t shown the appetite for the ground invasion needed to take out the Iranian government.

“I don't see any way around a ground invasion unless you're just planning on luck,” Connable said. “And luck in this case would be the Iranian economy collapses, or there's a revolt against the leadership, and that can't be predetermined.”

Connable also warned that Washington could stumble into a ground conflict without choosing one. A downed American aircraft could trigger a combat search-and-rescue operation involving hundreds of troops operating inside hostile territory.

Iranian officials, meanwhile, have warned that renewed attacks would not force Tehran to change its position.

"Recently, there has been talk of a new war, but I am already thinking about the post-war period,” Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Sunday during a televised event in Tehran, according to an Arab News translation. “Whether there is war or not, our policies remain the same."

Iran, meanwhile, has threatened to expand its retaliation beyond American military targets. Officials have warned that new strikes could trigger attacks on airports, pipelines, undersea internet cables and other civilian infrastructure across the Persian Gulf, as well as U.S. bases and warships.

Connable said he considers attacks on Gulf Arab states and commercial shipping particularly credible threats, because they are “less well defended than a warship” and because they could be used to “pump the price of oil back up again” and strengthen Tehran’s negotiating leverage.

Iranian officials have also suggested the war could expand. “Our strategy is ‘zero red lines,’” Mehdi Mohammadi, an adviser to Iran's nuclear negotiator, told The Guardian last week. “The war will continue longer and in a wider geographical area than the enemy anticipates.”

The threat is already prompting precautions. Axios reported that Jay Clayton, the director of national intelligence, warned Friday that Iran "substantially increased" its efforts to target American diplomats and officials in the Middle East and beyond, with lethal plots reaching "advanced stages.”

The State Department has ordered nonessential embassy personnel and their families to leave Saudi Arabia and has reduced staffing at other diplomatic posts in the region. The Pentagon withdrew about a dozen B-1 bombers from a British airbase this month following warnings of a possible Iranian-backed attack.

Connable warned of a threat that has yet to fully emerge: terrorist attacks by Iranian operatives or networks against Americans beyond the battlefield.

“That is a capacity they have; they have not demonstrated it,” Connable said. “The more desperate we make them, the more likely they are to resort to terrorism.”

entries.title: Ceasefire in Ukrainian City Brokered by Melania Trump Begins
entries.summary: A local pause in fighting started Tuesday to allow an aid mission into the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky this week.
entries.content:
By Hanna Arhirova

KHERSON, Ukraine (AP) — Russia and Ukraine began observing a localized ceasefire in a devastated southern Ukrainian city on Tuesday, ahead of a planned humanitarian mission the White House said was brokered by U.S. first lady Melania Trump. Moscow kept up its deadly missile attacks on other cities in the meantime.

Meanwhile, Finland’s president and Norway’s prime minister spoke by phone with Russian President Vladimir Putin, officials said, in their first known direct contact since shortly after Russia's all-out invasion of Ukraine began on Feb. 24, 2022.

Many Western officials have accused Putin of masterminding a campaign of disruption across Europe and have sought to diplomatically isolate the Russian leader.

Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre and Finnish President Alexander Stubb later spoke with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, according to Zelenskyy's office.

A ceasefire takes hold in a southern Ukraine city, officials say

A local pause in fighting started at 3 a.m. to allow an aid mission into the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky this week. Food and medical supplies are running perilously low in Oleshky, where drones and land mines restrict movement for the up to 2,000 people still there.

The humanitarian truce is a high-stakes operation for Moscow and Kyiv, with both sides keen to win U.S. President Donald Trump’s favor. Earlier attempts at limited ceasefires have quickly unraveled or never took hold due to the deep mistrust between Russia and Ukraine.

Russian and Ukrainian negotiators and their militaries confirmed in separate statements that the Oleshky ceasefire had begun.

Nordic leaders say Putin call was ‘frank and substantive’

The phone calls with the Russian and Ukrainian leaders followed an Oct. 20 meeting in Oslo between the two Nordic leaders, Zelenskyy and U.S. special envoy Steve Witkoff.

Stubb and Støre said they initiated the call with Putin, speaking with him for 90 minutes, to discuss the war and upcoming trilateral talks involving delegations from Russia, Ukraine and the United States that are expected to take place next month in Abu Dhabi, United Arab Emirates. The talks will seek to lay the groundwork for detailed peace negotiations.

The two European leaders spoke on behalf of their countries but not all of Europe, they said in statements.

“The discussion was frank and substantive,” Stubb said.

Denmark’s prime minister said she was “very skeptical” of reaching out to Putin, saying she sees “no signs that Russia desires peace with Europe” and noting that the call was not coordinated with other European leaders.

“I believe we should keep Europe united, rather than going it alone,” Mette Frederiksen said.

The Kremlin gave no hint that Moscow is ready to back down from its key demands, saying in a statement that “achieving a just and long-term peace is possible only if the legitimate interests of the Russian Federation are fully and unconditionally taken into account.”

Zelenskyy said Russian attacks, including relentless strikes on Ukraine’s power grid, must stop in order to open a path to peace.

“There must be peace, de-escalation is needed, and Russia must stop dragging out the war,” Zelenskyy said on X.

Melania Trump and Pope Leo worked for a truce in Oleshky

According to her office, Melania Trump led talks with civilian negotiators from Russia and Ukraine after meeting with U.N. officials who briefed her on the situation in Oleshky.

The partly occupied Kherson region of Ukraine that includes Oleshky has been subject to repeated Russian drone attacks on soldiers and civilians.

Pope Leo XIV spoke this month with Zelenskyy and Putin, urging them to allow humanitarian aid into Oleshky and the safe evacuation of civilians, the Vatican said.

Negotiators involved in the aid mission said doctors, medicines, food supplies and water would be taken to Oleshky before evacuation corridors are opened.

Moscow and Kyiv have blamed each other for the humanitarian crisis.

Under international law, the occupying power — Russia — must ensure civilians under its occupation live safely. Ukraine has repeatedly tried to negotiate with Moscow to establish a humanitarian corridor for evacuations and aid delivery.

Kherson residents take advantage of the lull in fighting

The local ceasefire is due to continue until 22:59 p.m. local time on Sunday, according to Davyd Arakhamia, a lawmaker with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy’s Servant of the People party.

Its geographical scope was unclear, though it was centered on Oleshky and other nearby parts of the Kherson region.

Oleshky is about 550 kilometers (340 miles) southeast of Kyiv, where the Dnipro River separates Russian and Ukrainian forces. Oleshky sits across the Dnipro River from the city of Kherson, the region’s administrative capital. Russian forces seized Kherson early in the full-scale invasion, but retreated across the river several months later.

In Kherson, the city streets were busier than usual and long lines formed at bus stops as residents used the truce to run errands.

“It’s unusual when it’s this quiet,” said Oleksandra Kostenko, who runs a small coffee kiosk. “We’re used to it being loud — the buzzing, the booming.”

But she fears Russia will use the lull to stockpile drones.

“It will end, and they will terrorize us,” Kostenko said.

Kherson bears the deep scars of war — windows boarded up, anti-drone nets stretched over streets and shattered glass littering sidewalks.

Yuliia Orlova was waiting for a bus to visit her mother in a district along the Dnipro that is usually too heavily shelled to reach.

“It seems quiet today, so I decided to go see my mom,” she said.

Russian missiles kill at least 3 civilians in Ukraine, officials say

Minutes after 3 a.m., multiple ballistic missile explosions shook Kyiv and air alerts sounded across the country.

Russian ballistic missiles damaged the grounds of a university in Kyiv, killing one person and leaving 12 wounded, city officials said. In Kharkiv, Ukraine's second-largest city, authorities said attacks late Monday killed two people and wounded four others.

In total, Russia launched 16 ballistic missiles and more than 280 drones at 11 regions of Ukraine, Zelenskyy said.

Susie Blann and Derek Gatopoulos contributed to this report from Kyiv.

entries.title: D.C.’s Teacher of the Year Calls Himself a ‘Griot’
entries.summary: Thurgood Marshall Academy’s Ramon Griffin uses creative strategies to reach students.
entries.content:
As he stepped into a small office at Thurgood Marshall Academy in Anacostia for an interview, Ramon Griffin reminded one student to get off their phone and convinced another to hand over a rice crispy snack.

It had been a long but exciting Monday for Griffin. That morning, Mayor Muriel Bowser and State Superintendent Dr. Antoinette S. Mitchell had named him D.C.’s Teacher of the Year.

He was recognized for his students’ “accelerated” academic growth and his unique teaching style. More than 87% of his students at Thurgood Marshall, a law-themed public charter school in Southeast Washington, passed the AP African American Studies exam during his first year teaching the course. Students in his math class surpassed their Measures of Academic Progress Growth expectations by up to 200%.

Griffin will represent the District in a national teacher competition and receive a $7,500 professional growth award.

“Mr. Griffin is the kind of educator every school hopes to have and every student deserves,” Elena Roberts, Thurgood Marshall’s head of school, said in a statement.

Griffin, who’s been teaching for 13 years, has spent the last seven at Thurgood Marshall. He likes to refer to himself as a “griot,” a West African term for a storyteller.

“I relate stories to the curriculum, which allows students to retain it,” he told The Sun.

“Being in class — especially 11th and 12th grade — you've been in school for so many years. You’re just tired,” said senior Ny’Zon O’Benson. “One thing about Griff’s class, I can go in there and just listen, and be like, OK, I mess with it.”

Griffin calls his journey to become an educator “layered and very deep.” He was born and raised in Detroit, after his grandparents moved to the Midwest during the Great Migration. He attributes his love of teaching and learning to his grandmother, who believed strongly in these virtues despite never graduating high school.

“I think about what our ancestors did not have, what our ancestors had to go through to sacrifice their lives and their bodies in order for us to be educated when at one time they were not,” said Griffin.

At Morehouse College, he considered child psychology and accounting, but the idea of teaching always stuck with him.

“It was my calling,” he said. “You have to believe in the universe. The universe will show you what your calling is.

Griffin often has his students arrange their desks in a circle.

“We're tribal,” he said. “We learn in a circular motion. We see face-to-face.”

Senior Armani Lindsey, a former math student of Griffin’s, considers him a mentor.

“That was the only class during that time where I felt like, all right, this cool,” Lindsey said. I got a great teacher, so I'm gonna be able to pass this. And I did pass.”

O’Benson attributes Griffin’s teaching success to his heart.

“He really wants to see the kids do better, because I drove him crazy,” he said, laughing.

He said Griffin stood beside him through a rough patch in his life, later helping him pass his AP exam.

Both Lindsey and O’Benson said they plan to apply to Morehouse College because of Griffin. Lindsey said he credits the teacher with expanding his worldview.

“I think Ward 8 is a very misrepresented world across the city,” Lindsey said. “It’s a lot of educators [here], but I think it's not a lot of educators that really truly care for the students and want to see the students move out of this area and do better for themselves. … That's one thing I will say: Mr. Griffin, he does.”

entries.title: The Sphere Is Officially Coming to Maryland
entries.summary: Prince George’s County approved the plan for the 6,000-seat venue Tuesday.
entries.content:
Prince George’s County will be home to the nation’s second Sphere, after the plan for the $1.4 billion entertainment venue got final approval from the county council on Tuesday.

The Sphere National Harbor, a smaller version of the famed Las Vegas venue, will bring a 6,000-seat theater equipped with high-resolution displays and an exterior LED screen to the banks of the Potomac River. Prince George’s County Council unanimously approved the project Tuesday, agreeing to issue $215 million in bonds to the developers. Sphere Entertainment Company will gradually repay that sum to the county.

Construction is expected to begin next year, with a planned opening in 2030, according to Sphere Entertainment. Internal estimates show the venue will create 1,750 on-site construction jobs and support an additional 2,400 through suppliers. The venue will have 328 full-time jobs and 925 part-time positions once it opens, according to the company.

The county council earlier this month shot down a proposal to require 40% of construction labor to come from unionized workers. It did pass an agreement that will allow union groups to organize Sphere workers once the venue opens.

Early estimates project 2 million annual visitors to the Sphere. County Executive Aisha Braveboy previously said the Sphere would bring $67 million in annual tax revenue — three times more than the combined tax revenue from Six Flags amusement park in Bowie, which closed last year, and Northwest Stadium, which the Commanders are leaving to move back to D.C.

If all timelines stay on track, the National Harbor venue will be the third Sphere in the world. Sphere Entertainment Co. is currently working on a 20,000-seat venue in Abu Dhabi, expected to be completed in 2029.

entries.title: Judge Orders Greg Abbott to Hand Over His Communications With Elon Musk
entries.summary: Several of Musk’s companies are based in Texas, including SpaceX, Tesla and X.
entries.content:
A federal judge in Texas has ordered the state’s Republican Gov. Greg Abbott to let his Democratic opponent review more than a thousand pages of unredacted emails between himself and Tesla CEO Elon Musk.

In a ruling on Monday, Travis County Judge Catherine Mauzy said state Rep. Gina Hinojosa is entitled to review the documents because she may use them for legislative reasons. Lawmakers are permitted to view executive branch communications under the Texas Public Information Act.

“Abbott has obstructed and continues to obstruct plaintiff Hinojosa’s exercise of her right to inspect the documents,” Mauzy wrote, calling Abbott’s conduct “illegal” under Texas law.

The governor's office was directed to turn the documents over to Hinojosa by 10 a.m. on Oct. 29. However, Abbott’s office has appealed the decision and won’t need to hand over the documents until the appeals process is over.

According to the filing, Hinojosa sought the emails to evaluate existing laws and potential legislative measures concerning the state government and economic-development incentives, state grants, business regulation, environmental protection and other matters affecting Elon Musk’s companies.

Several of Musk’s companies are based in Texas, including SpaceX, Tesla and X.

Sign up for The Stakeout, The Sun's Congress newsletter you actually want to read. 

In a 2024 X post, Musk said he was moving SpaceX from Hawthorne, California, to Starbase, Texas, because of the state’s anti-transgender laws. Musk has a transgender daughter, Vivian Wilson, who has become an outspoken critic of her father.

In 2020, Musk announced he’d be moving Tesla from California to Texas after Alameda County, where Tesla had been based, barred the company from resuming production during the COVID-19 pandemic.

In both instances, Musk called the policies the “final straw.”

A news release from Hinojosa’s office says Abbott tried to withhold the emails because they were too “intimate and embarrassing.”

“Texans built this great state, and we aren’t going to let Abbott’s donors continue buying up our land, shutting down our schools, or taking our water and electricity for their benefit,” Hinojosa said in a news release following the ruling.

“The people have the right to transparency, and that’s why I’m continuing to fight for the documents between Elon Musk and Greg Abbott,” she added.

In an emailed statement to The Washington Sun, Andrew Mahaleris, Abbott’s press secretary, called the lawsuit “a baseless stunt and nothing more than an act of desperation.”

Mahaleris accused Hinojosa of abusing her capacity for political purposes. The governor’s office has also filed a motion to dismiss the lawsuit.

Hinojosa first requested to inspect the emails on Sept. 29, specifically asking the governor’s office for correspondence that took place before Oct. 13.

Abbott did not allow Hinojosa to inspect the emails, the ruling states, despite Hinojosa offering to comply with Texas confidentiality protections.

On Oct. 19, Hinojosa filed a lawsuit against Abbott for refusing to let her inspect the documents.

Hinojosa noted some of the emails had been sent to The Texas Newsroom.

The governor’s office provided nearly 1,400 pages of emails to the outlet; all but 200 pages were unredacted or blacked out.

None of the emails have been made public.

Abbott has given Musk’s companies billions of dollars in state grants and tax breaks, per the news release. Musk reportedly benefited from a $1.66 billion tax break after the tech tycoon donated $500,000 to Abbott’s reelection campaign.

A hearing is scheduled for Nov. 2 to determine whether the court should issue a temporary injunction against Abbott.

entries.title: The Shadow of Trump’s Arch Would Stretch Across D.C. Memorials
entries.summary: A Washington Post model found the arch’s shadow would cover Arlington National Cemetery graves on 284 days a year.
entries.content:
President Donald Trump’s proposed 250-foot Triumphal Arch would cast a shadow over presidential memorials, war monuments and thousands of graves each year, according to a digital 3D model created by The Washington Post.

Construction on Trump’s arch could start on Nov. 5 pending final approval from a federal commission stacked with his own appointees. Planned to be built in a traffic circle situated between D.C. and Arlington, the massive structure would change the capital’s visual landscape, breaking up the relatively open air between Arlington National Cemetery and the National Mall.

As the sun rises and sets, the arch’s shadow would move along with it, covering burial sites at the cemetery on 284 days each year, the Post found. The shadow would pass over more than 75,000 graves.

The shadow would recede from the cemetery before it opens most days, but would linger during operating hours on 26 days, the Post reported.

The Interior Department called the Post’s analysis “flawed” in a statement to The Washington Sun, saying its own internal modeling is more reliable.

The design team in charge of the arch project ran its own solar models and found a period of less than two weeks, at the beginning of daylight saving time, when the arch’s shadow would fall over a portion of the cemetery while it's open, the Interior Department said.

The Interior Department said it studied the shadow at 8 a.m. (when the cemetery opens), 9 a.m., noon and 3 p.m. on a handful of days throughout the year.

The Post analyzed the shadow on each day of the year and included times when the cemetery is closed to the public.

The arch has faced multiple legal challenges, including a lawsuit filed by three Vietnam War veterans who argue its construction would, among other things, obstruct the view of Arlington National Cemetery. Local preservation officials have pushed back against the monument, saying Trump administration officials have underestimated how much the “integrity of the affected historic properties would be diminished” by its construction.

The arch’s shadow would cast across Arlington Memorial Bridge and linger over the Lincoln Memorial during the fall and winter, the Post found. In the spring and summer, the shadow would fall on John F. Kennedy’s grave.

The shadow would also fall onto parts of the Martin Luther King Jr. Memorial on more than 30 days of the year, and at times cover the Vietnam and Korean war memorials, the Post found.

The National Park Service previously outlined dozens of historic sites the arch would affect, but said the project should move forward as planned. The park service declined to consider alternate locations for the monument, calling the location “central to the undertaking” of the construction.

Arlington County sued to stop construction earlier this month, arguing the Trump administration failed to complete a legally required environmental review process before barreling ahead with development.

The arch received an early approval from the U.S. Commission of Fine Arts, a board packed with Trump appointees. The National Capital Planning Commission will consider final approval for the project on Nov. 5.

entries.title: WNBA Players Don’t Have to Go Overseas Anymore. Lauren Betts Did Anyway.
entries.summary: Higher salaries mean that WNBA players no longer have to chase offseason paychecks in Europe or Asia. But the Mystics’ center saw a chance to develop her game.
entries.content:
This has been a year without an offseason for Lauren Betts.

Her college season ran through March Madness and into April as she won a national championship with UCLA. Less than two weeks after cutting down the nets, Betts was drafted No. 4 overall by the Mystics, and training camp started just a few days later. She played all 44 games of the WNBA regular season. Betts kept at it until the Mystics’ run ended in the first round of the playoffs. Finally, as September turned to October, she was done.

For a day.

Well, two days, technically. And then she flew to Turkey to start playing with EuroLeague powerhouse Fenerbahçe in Istanbul.

“I'm really big on balance, and you know, there were some points I did tell myself, like, I just want to take a break from basketball,” Betts said the day after the Mystics’ season ended and two days before she left for Turkey. “But I feel like I would be doing a disservice to myself if I didn’t just continue to grow. And I feel like going to Turkey and playing overseas is going to be a really good opportunity for me.”

That used to be the norm in the WNBA. Most players spent years going straight from one basketball season in the U.S. to another in Europe or Asia. It meant developing their games, but it also meant picking up a crucial paycheck. That dynamic has changed as the sport has experienced record growth over the past few years, with players unlocking higher salaries and more choices on how to build their careers. It has become far less common for high-profile young Americans like Betts to spend the winter playing in Europe.

But it was an experience she’d always wanted to have.

Some WNBA players have talked about how much they value the opportunity to spend their offseasons in the U.S. Betts valued the opportunity to go somewhere else.

Her father, Andy, spent years playing basketball in Spain, with other stints in Italy, Greece and Ukraine. (He was drafted by the Charlotte Hornets as the No. 50 pick in 1998 but never appeared in the NBA.) His career led to an early childhood full of travel and cultural experiences for Betts and her siblings.

The family returned to the U.S. when she began third grade. She grew up in suburban Colorado, but she never forgot how enchanting she found those early years in Europe.

“I’m basically just fulfilling the family legacy,” Betts said with a smile. “It’s kind of full circle that I’m doing the same thing I watched my dad do.”

None of the American players chosen as lottery picks in 2024 or 2025 have spent their WNBA offseasons playing overseas. Betts is the only one from 2026 to do so with a traditional basketball team. (Top pick Azzi Fudd has signed on with the start-up Project B, which plans to stage a traveling global tournament beginning in January.) Some of these players have chosen to use their offseasons for rest or private development. Many have chosen to join Unrivaled, a 3-on-3 league that began play in Miami in 2025, which lets them earn another salary and work on their games while remaining in the U.S.

“I think we’re privileged now that we have so many options as women,” Mystics forward Michaela Onyenwere said at the end of the season. “We don’t have to go overseas for a full seven months. I’m very grateful for that.”

Onyenwere entered the WNBA in 2021. She spent her first several winters playing in Spain, Turkey and China, joining many of her peers in figuring out how to navigate different international leagues every offseason. But this year, for the first time in her pro career, Onyenwere felt comfortable ending one season without immediate plans to jump into another.

WNBA paychecks increased significantly this year under a new collective bargaining agreement. Minimum salaries went from roughly $66,000 in 2025 to $270,000 in 2026. (The average player earned about $580,000 — roughly quadruple the average from a year ago.) It also helps that players have seen an uptick in endorsement deals as the league has grown in popularity. Getting another paycheck in the winter no longer feels quite so necessary. For a more established, mid-career player like Onyenwere, that creates an opportunity to spend the offseason truly off.

But the chance to practice against top international competition was still a draw for Betts. Her decision to join Fenerbahçe was about development as much as it was about family tradition. A 6-foot-7 center, Betts showed growth in her rookie year, picking up extra minutes as the season wore on and becoming a more assertive rebounder. But she knows that she needs to sharpen her footwork and become more comfortable outside the paint.

Through her first two games with Fenerbahçe, Betts is averaging 11 points, 8.5 rebounds and two assists.

“Any chance that I can just get myself into uncomfortable situations and just grow my game and try to put the ball on the floor a little more, shoot a little more,” Betts said before she left for Turkey. “I feel like it's another opportunity for me to just get better and gain more confidence.”

That, she figured, would be worth staying in season for a few extra months.

entries.title: The Other Dan Sullivan Is Deep in Debt Amid Legal Battle
entries.summary: Confusion reigns in Alaska’s costly U.S. Senate race where two candidates — including the incumbent — have the same name.
entries.content:
Legal trouble facing the Alaska U.S. Senate candidate Daniel J. Sullivan is getting expensive.

Daniel J. Sullivan — not to be confused with incumbent Sen. Dan Sullivan, who’s on the same ballot — is more than $21,000 in debt for “compliance and legal fees,” according to Federal Election Commission filings reviewed by The Washington Sun.

Daniel J. Sullivan’s campaign ran into legal trouble in June, when the Alaska Division of Elections disqualified him from appearing on the open primary election ballot. Election officials alleged Sullivan was running in bad faith and his name would confuse voters supporting incumbent Sen. Dan Sullivan.

The case, fast-tracked ahead of the state’s primary vote, rose to the Alaska Supreme Court, which struck down the election officials’ decision and ruled Sullivan must remain on the ballot on June 29.

In a July Facebook post, Daniel J. Sullivan called the case “frivolous” and said he’d spent thousands of dollars to “simply to defend my right to remain on the ballot.” He included a fundraising link in his post.

“When I decided to run for the U.S. Senate, I intended to do so without asking anyone for money,” he wrote. “I believed that sharing a simple message—that twelve years of Senator Sullivan is enough and that Alaska deserves better—would not require a fundraising campaign.”

Daniel J. Sullivan did not respond to The Sun’s requests for comment.

FEC filings confirm that Daniel J. Sullivan is in debt for legal fees. As of Oct. 14, his campaign owes $21,399 to the Washington law firm Caplin & Drysdale, which did not respond to The Sun’s request for comment before publication.

The Anchorage office of law firm Ballard Spahr, which court documents list as representing Daniel J. Sullivan in the June lawsuit, also did not respond to The Sun’s request for comment. (The Sun receives legal counsel from Ballard Spahr’s Washington office.)

According to FEC filings, Daniel J. Sullivan’s campaign also borrowed $10,400 from the candidate himself in June and July, when his case was being litigated, bringing the campaign’s total debt up to over $30,000.

As of Oct. 14, Daniel J. Sullivan’s campaign reported just $1,901 cash on hand.

“These legal challenges have consumed valuable time and financial resources that I never imagined would become part of running for public office,” Daniel J. Sullivan wrote in his post. “If candidates can be burdened with costly legal battles simply for seeking office, it discourages qualified citizens from running and limits the choices available to voters.”

Despite the June ruling, Sullivan the senator, whose campaign had over $2 million cash on hand as of mid-October, continued to rail against the other Sullivan’s candidacy, accusing him of being a Democratic Party plant designed to pull votes away from the incumbent Republican.
Dan.Sullivan.Trump (5152x3434, AR: 1.50)Other Republicans piled on. The National Republican Senatorial Campaign sent a letter to the Alaska Division of Elections before the June case was heard to oppose Sullivan’s candidacy. President Donald Trump dubbed Daniel J. Sullivan “Decoy Dan” and vowed during an October visit to Alaska to use federal resources to investigate the candidate.

Trump kept his word: A week later, the Department of Justice filed a complaint against the Alaska Division of Elections (which originally knocked Daniel J. Sullivan off the ballot in June). Trump wrote in a Truth Social post a few days before the lawsuit was filed that the other Sullivan is “totally unrelated to Politics.”

“It’s ridiculous that the Court didn’t stop this SCAM,” he wrote.

On the November ballot, Daniel J. Sullivan’s name is listed without any party label. Sen. Dan Sullivan’s name is listed as “Dan S. Sullivan (Registered Republican) Incumbent.”

The nonincumbent Sullivan isn’t a named party in the lawsuit by the federal government, but his candidacy is still the subject of this brewing election-integrity fight.

Harry Child, a spokesperson for Democratic candidate Mary Peltola’s campaign, said the lawsuit is “a despicable political threat” and attributed it to “Senator Dan Sullivan’s allies.”

Peltola’s campaign currently has over $4 million in cash on hand as of Oct. 14, according to FEC filings.

Daniel J. Sullivan hasn’t filed an amicus brief in the new lawsuit, and it’s unclear if he plans to get involved.

entries.title: Federal Agents Raid Beverly Hills Mansion Tied to Eric Swalwell
entries.summary: Five women accused the former congressman of sexual assault and harassment earlier this year.
entries.content:
Federal agents raided a Beverly Hills mansion connected to Eric Swalwell early Tuesday morning as part of an investigation into the former congressman, according to multiple reports.

In an emailed statement to The Washington Sun, the FBI said it “conducted an operation in the Los Angeles region related to an ongoing criminal investigation. We have no further comment.”

Swalwell, a Democrat, resigned from Congress in April and dropped out of the California governor’s race after five women accused him of sexual assault and harassment. He has vowed to “fight the serious, false allegation against me.”

As part of a probe into Swalwell’s conduct, FBI agents seized his electronics earlier this year at the San Francisco International Airport, according to the Los Angeles Times. Authorities in Los Angeles County and New York are pursuing different investigations, the outlet reported.

Federal authorities also raided Swalwell’s Washington home in August as part of the investigation.

The Washington Sun has contacted Swalwell for comment.

According to the Los Angeles Times, the home raided by authorities on Tuesday belongs to billionaire Stephen Cloobeck, who dropped out of the California governor race and endorsed Swalwell’s run for the office.

Swalwell stayed at Cloobeck’s home and used it for political events and campaigning, according to the newspaper. He was kicked out of the residence after the sexual assault allegations came to light.

The raid is an escalation in ongoing probes tied to Swalwell’s time in office.

It also comes as the Justice Department ramps up legal action against several Democrats ahead of the midterm elections, breaking with the decades-long precedent of avoiding politically charged cases shortly before Election Day.

Last week, the DOJ charged Virginia state Sen. Louise Lucas as part of a public corruption case involving her cannabis business. She has vowed to fight the case, saying in a statement: “I grew up under Jim Crow. I’ve seen what happens when people in power try to silence those who stand up to them.”

“I spent my life fighting back, and I’m not stopping now,” she added.

And earlier this month, Department of Homeland Security agents raided Rep. Ilhan Omar’s Washington, D.C., home as part of an “ongoing federal criminal investigation,” which officials suggested was related to immigration. She has likewise promised to fight the Trump administration on any case that arises.

“Make no mistake: this is an attempt to target political enemies and weaponize federal law enforcement. For ten years, Trump has targeted me with baseless lies and smear campaigns. This is just the latest escalation in his campaign of political intimidation,” she said. “I will not be silenced.”

entries.title: Mike Waltz Gets Into a Shouting Match With Top Cuban Official at the U.N.
entries.summary: The General Assembly gaveled out of session to diffuse the spat.
entries.content:
Mike Waltz, the U.S. ambassador to the United Nations, got into a shouting match with Cuba’s minister of foreign affairs, Bruno Rodríguez Parrilla, on the floor of the General Assembly on Tuesday.

In footage that circulated on social media, Rodríguez Parrilla is seen approaching the assembly stage as Waltz says, “This individual needs to back away from this podium. He's not going to intimidate me in the United States of America like he tries to intimidate political prisoners.”

An official in the clip responds, “This individual is the foreign minister for the Republic of Cuba.”

Waltz responds, pounding his fist on the podium and raising his voice, “And I’m the representative for the United States of America. Back up.”

Rodríguez Parrilla then shouts, “You are a liar.”

In a statement posted to social media, Waltz said, “The Castro regime has profited at the expense of the Cuban people with luxury cars, expensive watches and a private island resort. As I shared this with the world, regime thugs rushed the stage to interrupt my speech.”

“They can intimidate their own people in Cuba but think again about trying that nonsense in the United States of America,” he added.

Footage of Waltz’s speech shows him discussing the effects of the Castro regime.

“When Castro sent thousands of gay people, Christians, Afro-Cubans and others to concentration camps, it was the regime who stripped them of their property,” Waltz said as Cuban officials banged their hands on their desks.

“I hope everyone, Mr. President, is listening to the delegation right now,” Waltz continued.

The Cuban delegation then requested a point of order.

Khalilur Rahman, the president of the U.N. General Assembly, requested that Waltz be able to conclude his speech before allowing Cuban officials to raise their objections.

But Rodríguez Parrilla walked toward the podium as Rahman struggled to maintain decorum. As Waltz and Rodríguez Parrill continued their shouting match, Rahman announced he’d be suspending the meeting.

entries.title: The Government’s Watchdog Agency Is Cutting Staff
entries.summary: The Government Accountability Office is facing budget issues, leading to delays in its oversight work.
entries.content:
The government’s official watchdog is looking to shed staff as it faces a budget crunch, increasing the potential for delays in its investigatory work.

The Government Accountability Office has offered incentives for its employees to leave, telling staff it expects to approve 200 departures. Eligible employees can take a buyout of up to $25,000, early retirement or a roughly three-month period of paid leave before leaving government.

The reduction would mark a 6% cut to the GAO’s workforce and a 11% drop in staff since President Donald Trump took office. The GAO is a legislative branch agency that Trump does not control. Congress sets its budget each year.

The agency said in a memo to staff that “we do not expect our operations will be adversely affected” by the staff reductions, as they would be taken across a broad cross section of its workforce. It added that it can shift around operational responsibilities as needed.

But the agency has already been struggling to handle the influx of investigations. One GAO employee said lawmakers requesting investigations from the agency are waiting weeks or months for staff to become available. The watchdog has taken steps to reduce those waits, the employee added, but eventually those will “not overcome the continued decline in staffing levels.”

“Smaller and slower — because of agency access issues — has basically been the vibe,” the employee said.

The separation incentives “will help GAO adjust to the current budget environment while continuing to serve the Congress, support our strategic plan, and meet mission needs,” Sarah Kaczmarek, a GAO spokesperson, said in a statement. “This is a prudent approach to ensure that we maintain capacity to meet Congressional priorities over time.”

The cuts come as the GAO is facing unusual pushback from federal agencies as it conducts its oversight work. The Trump administration has directed agencies to limit the access it grants the GAO, and the watchdog has noted in numerous reports that agencies were noncompliant. The GAO has also repeatedly cited the administration for flouting federal spending laws by unlawfully withholding or rescinding appropriated funds.

The watchdog agency has seen flat funding for two years after lawmakers pushed back on dramatic cuts proposed by House Republicans. GAO leaders are now telling staff that the agency cannot sustain its current staffing levels without a funding boost. If an insufficient number of volunteers sign up to leave, they said, involuntary layoffs would be issued as a “last resort.”

The GAO told staff the number of employees it approves to leave could be subject to change. It offered separation incentives to its workforce last year, but this is the first time it has offered the extended paid leave option.

A post-Watergate law gave the GAO authority to sue an administration that improperly refuses to spend money, though the GAO has not done so in decades. The Washington Sun previously reported that the White House has floated naming one of its own officials, Office of Management and Budget Deputy Director Eric Ueland, to lead the agency.

Congressional Democrats are promising extensive oversight of the Trump administration if they regain control of either House of Congress, which could lead to a surge of work for the GAO.

entries.title: Brazilian Presidential Candidate Flávio Bolsonaro Flees to the U.S. Following Loss
entries.summary: Bolsonaro, the son of the country’s former president Jair Bolsonaro, was ordered to remain in Brazil while a money-laundering investigation proceeded.
entries.content:
Brazilian Senator Flávio Bolsonaro has reportedly fled the country following his presidential election loss over the weekend, in an apparent attempt to avoid a federal corruption investigation into his family enterprises.

The politician was reportedly on a plane to Florida as of 3 p.m. Tuesday, according to U.S. and Brazilian officials who spoke with CNN. The network reported that Bolsonaro had feared arrest in Brazil, where the country’s Supreme Court ordered him to surrender his passports and barred him from international travel as part of a criminal probe into a $10 million money-laundering and corruption scheme. He has denied wrongdoing.

Talk of Bolsonaro's clandestine escape was first published by the Argentine news outlet Infobae, which reported he crossed the border into Argentina after losing his presidential bid against President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva on Sunday. Argentine officials reported “no record” of Bolsonaro entering the country.

Following his defeat, Bolsonaro took to Instagram on Monday to address the court order to surrender his passports. He said in a video that Brazilian police informed him of the exit ban in person.

“I never thought about leaving the country,” he said at the time. “I will hand over my passports and defend myself against this outrage, which is clearly an attempt to intimidate me. But no one will silence me.”

Rather than address the accusations directly, Bolsonaro connected the federal probe to the election results. In his statements, he accused Lula of staging an attempt to interfere in the election and slammed Brazilian media as a fake news “industrial complex” designed to “terrorize” the masses.

If Bolsonaro does touch down in the U.S. and is allowed to stay, he will join a group of Brazilian conservative political refugees in exile in the United States, including the country’s former intelligence chief Alexandre Ramagem and his brother Eduardo Bolsonaro, who warned him on a podcast to “leave the country” two days earlier.

On Tuesday morning, Eduardo Bolsonaro denied allegations that his brother had fled Brazil.

It’s unclear what reception Flávio Bolsonaro will receive in the U.S., though President Donald Trump has been a steadfast ally to his father, Jair Bolsonaro, and said this week that he believed Brazil’s presidential election had been rigged against Flávio.

“It looked like another rigged election, frankly,” he told reporters Monday. “I didn't take sides, I didn't endorse anybody or anything, but I watched the election. It looks so, so corrupt, so terrible."

entries.title: Rock Legend Hits Trump’s Campaign Arm With $10M Copyright Lawsuit
entries.summary: Neil Young also filed a similar lawsuit in 2020.
entries.content:
Rock ’n’ roll legend Neil Young is suing President Donald Trump for $10 million after the president’s team played one of his songs at a recent rally.

As Trump walked onto the stage at the Covelli Centre in Youngstown, Ohio, on Oct. 12, Young’s song “Rockin’ in the Free World” played in the background.

Trump was not granted permission to play the song at the event, according to the copyright infringement lawsuit, filed Monday in U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of Virginia. Young is suing Trump 47 Committee Inc., the president’s joint fundraising committee.

“The Committee does not now have, and did not at the time of the Youngstown Rally or any other rally financed and conducted by the Committee, have a license or Young’s permission to play the Song at any public political event,” the suit states.

Young claims the song was also played at other Trump rallies.

According to the court filings, Trump’s campaign knew it needed a license to play the song and knew Young would not permit it to use his music.

The song portrays the contrasts between the “promises of American political rhetoric” and the “harsh realities faced by the poor, homeless and forgotten,” the suit states.

“In short, the Song is the opposite of everything Donald J. Trump stands for.”

Young sued Donald J. Trump for President Inc. for copyright infringement in 2020 over “Rockin’ in the Free World” and “Devil’s Sidewalk.”

In that instance, the entity asserted no defense and quickly settled the suit, promising not to play the song again without a license and permission, according to the new lawsuit.

“The Committee has willfully proceeded to cause the Song to be played despite its lack of a license and despite its knowledge that a license is required to do so,” the lawsuit states.

The Washington Sun contacted the White House for comment.

Several other notable musicians have objected to the use of their music for Trump’s rallies. Others have also taken legal action against the president.

In 2024, the Trump campaign settled a lawsuit filed by “Electric Avenue" singer Eddy Grant after the song appeared in a social media post during the 2020 campaign.

The White Stripes sued the Trump campaign in 2024 after their song “Seven Nation Army” was also used in a social media video posted by campaign deputy director of communications Margo Martin.

entries.title: Judges Knock DOJ for the Late Timing of Election Lawsuits
entries.summary: With more last-minute litigation apparently ahead, judges already say the Trump administration could have acted sooner.
entries.content:
With a week left until Election Day and millions of ballots already cast, federal judges are airing not-so-subtle skepticism about the timing of the Trump administration’s recent election lawsuits against states.

In rulings in unrelated cases late Monday, judges in California and Alaska pointed out that Justice Department officials had waited months to sue state election administrators over issues that had been on their radar since at least early summer.

The judges signaled they were unsympathetic to the DOJ’s demands for speedy rulings, noting that officials had ample time to act but filed their challenges only after many ballots had been mailed and processed.

"That these proceedings encroach on the cusp of an election," U.S. Circuit Judge Gabriel Sanchez of California wrote separately in an order, "is a delay entirely of the United States’ own making."

In California, Sanchez and Judge Mark Bennett of the 9th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals were the 2-1 majority in an order that shot down the Justice Department’s bid to more quickly force state and local election officials to set aside 20,000 mail ballots the administration claims are for potential noncitizens.

The opinion noted that Department of Homeland Security officials first sent their analysis of alleged noncitizens on voter rolls to the state in July. When state officials asked the administration for details about the methodology, the administration didn’t respond. Hearing nothing further, election officials mailed ballots at the beginning of October, as required by state law.

The administration had all the information it needed to file suit “well before” mid-October — 10 days after California counties could begin counting and months after the original notification — the order says, adding that the administration’s “claimed emergency, at least in part, is a self-constructed one.”

The DOJ attorneys in the lawsuit initially asked for a ruling by Election Day on their request for an order. Then, shortly before 9 p.m. on Oct. 21, they demanded an expedited ruling by noon the next day — effectively giving the district court three business hours to rule, the order says.

The district court hadn’t yet ruled when the lawyers filed an appeal to the 9th Circuit. The DOJ’s sense of urgency appeared to have been driven in part by a sudden realization that Los Angeles County had processed 331,000 ballots and that counting was well underway, according to the 9th Circuit’s order.

“That the United States had overlooked the fact that counties across California would be working diligently to process ballots for the millions of voters residing within the State does not equal inaction by the district court or circumstances outside the United States’s control,” the opinion read.

In the Alaska case, lawyers for Democrats and voting advocacy groups pointed to the Trump administration's suspect timing in asking to speedily consider dismissing the DOJ's lawsuit before the election — and a federal judge agreed.

U.S. District Judge Sharon Gleason noted that months had passed since the Alaska Supreme Court had cleared the way for two Senate candidates named Dan Sullivan to appear on the state’s ballot. Sample ballots went out over the summer, the primary was held without issue in August, and no other legal challenges had been filed over the listing of names on the ballot, the judge wrote.

"After Alaskans had already begun casting their ballots for the November 2026 election — and nearly four months after the Alaska Supreme Court directed the Division of Elections to include Daniel J. Sullivan on the ballot for the upcoming United States Senate election — the United States initiated this action on October 22, 2026," she wrote.

The judge set a blisteringly fast pace for federal litigation, with filing deadlines that set up a potential decision on the motions to dismiss by Thursday night.

Democratic officials at the state and federal level said they expect the Justice Department to expand its 11th-hour legal maneuvering in the coming days. In court papers Monday, they asked a judge to block the DOJ from ordering state and local election officials to remove specific voters from their rolls prior to Nov. 3.

The motion, filed on behalf of the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee and other Democratic groups, also asks the court to prohibit the DOJ from forcing election administrators to withhold or set aside ballots.

Shortly before the motion was filed, the Justice Department set another potential legal challenge in motion in the state of Washington. In a Monday letter to Secretary of State Steve Hobbs, the DOJ claims the state has more than 400 noncitizens who voted in U.S. elections. Similarly to California, the DOJ gave Washington a tight deadline to comply with checking the citizenship of those listed.

The letter even acknowledges the time constraints and the looming midterm elections. The DOJ gave the state a deadline of noon Wednesday, adding: “If you cannot implement this process by then, given the ongoing federal election, the United States will have no choice but to seek emergency relief.”

When asked by a reporter on Thursday whether the DOJ would continue bringing litigation to other states, Attorney General Todd Blanche said, “Maybe.”

“It depends. There’s a number of states that we’re looking at. So, whether we’re gonna do something before the election, I don’t want to get ahead of the civil lawyers working on those cases,” Blanche added. “But yes, if we have the same information from other states I expect we’ll move.”

Justice Department spokesperson Kiersten Pels declined to comment on the pending litigation and did not address a question seeking to clarify Blanche’s remarks.

In an emailed statement, she said it was the department’s job to prevent noncitizens from voting. “When our federal partners identify individuals who, with a high level of confidence, are or were noncitizens and have cast ballots, the Department will act, and it will not wait for a more convenient time,” she said.

Justin Levitt, a constitutional scholar at Loyola Law School, said the Justice Department’s cases thus far appeared to be based less on a coherent legal strategy and more on an effort to keep the administration’s contested claims of ballot problems in the news.

“Most of them are press releases rather than cases. They just happen to have court docket numbers on them,” Levitt said in an interview. “What they've done so far in this administration is really just get themselves in the press for 24 hours and survive until they can figure out what to do next.”

entries.title: A Top House Democrat Says His Party Is United on the Economy
entries.summary: Rep. Pete Aguilar, the number three House Democrat, said Democrats plan to focus first on legislation to lower costs if they win control.
entries.content:
Rep. Pete Aguilar, who is positioned to become the House majority whip if Democrats reclaim the chamber in November, said party leaders are already thinking through how to unite an ideologically diverse caucus behind an agenda focused on lowering costs and combating corruption.

But a week before Election Day, the California Democrat cautioned against a guaranteed victory.

“Nothing's inevitable. We got to win elections,” Aguilar said in an interview from South Texas, where he was campaigning for Rep. Henry Cuellar. “We got to win first.”

Aguilar, the highest ranking Latino in Congress, has been on the campaign trail helping candidates, especially those in areas with large Hispanic populations, ahead of Election Day. He has visited Pennsylvania in support of Janelle Stelson and Bob Brooks, New Jersey in support of Rep. Nellie Pou and candidate Rebecca Bennett, and New York in support of Rep. Laura Gillen.

Should Democrats secure the majority, Aguilar pointed to three broad priorities to address: lowering everyday costs, addressing health care access and lowering caregiving expenses. He also vowed Democrats would address corruption issues within President Donald Trump's administration. That would also include investigations from relevant House committees and legislation to ban lawmakers from trading stocks.

“I would anticipate that Leader [Hakeem] Jeffries will talk about the process for the affirmative agenda and what we plan to carry forward,” Aguilar said, pointing to the minority leader’s discussions of the first 100 hours and first 100 days of a Democratic majority.

Aguilar ticked off a list of items a new majority would focus on. “The rising costs that people face are crushing them: housing, health care, gas, groceries, utilities, child care, elder care and then corruption,” Aguilar said. “Those are going to be the elements of what the agenda kind of looks like in the first 100 hours [and] the first 100 days.”

But the path to turning those priorities into law could be difficult. Aguilar told The Washington Sun that even if Democrats retake the House, the Senate's 60-vote threshold for advancing most legislation would remain a significant obstacle, regardless of which party controls the upper chamber. And Trump will still occupy the White House for the next two years.

“In my opinion no party is sniffing anywhere near 60 for a while, and so we're going to have to work,” he said.

He said the priority for Democrats was to move what they can from the lower chamber.

“We'll have an agenda. We'll focus and we'll move that off of the House floor, and then we'll send it over to the Senate,” he said. “No matter what the Senate looks like, we can engage.”

He acknowledged the party has seen ideological differences emerge in primary contests, raising questions about how a potentially narrow majority could complicate leaders’ efforts to get different factions on the same page. He said Democrats are currently focused on winning the competitive districts that will determine control of the chamber.

“Right now the elections that matter, the elections that give us an ability to make Hakeem Jeffries speaker, are the races that we're focused on, not bright blue districts,” he said. “We'll govern to find that highest common denominator of what's the most that we can possibly do, and we'll chart our efforts to get there.”

That balancing act could become particularly important if Democrats secure only a slim majority, leaving party leaders little room for defections.

Aguilar expressed confidence in Jeffries' readiness to lead the chamber, while emphasizing that the minority leader remains focused on the immediate task of winning the election.

“He's prepared and he will do well, but he also isn't measuring the drapes right now,” Aguilar said. “He's doing everything he can to make sure that these candidates have the resources and the energy down the home stretch.”

For now, Aguilar said Democrats are concentrating on the final days of campaigning, particularly in competitive districts that could determine whether Jeffries gets the speaker's gavel.

“We're going to sprint through the finish,” he said. “We got a lot of work to do here in the Rio Grande Valley, here in South Texas, but we feel good about where we are across the board.”

entries.title: U.S. Military Says 5 Were Killed by a Strike on an Alleged Drug Boat in the Pacific
entries.summary: The latest attack brings the number of people who have been killed by the U.S. military's boat strikes to at least 240 in more than 70 strikes.
entries.content:
By Ben Finley

The U.S. military said it attacked a boat it accused of smuggling drugs in the eastern Pacific Ocean on Tuesday, killing five people, as the Trump administration continues its campaign against alleged traffickers in Latin America.

The latest attack brings the number of people who have been killed by the U.S. military's boat strikes to at least 240 in more than 70 strikes. The Trump administration began targeting those it calls “narcoterrorists” in September 2025.

As with most of the military’s statements on strikes in the eastern Pacific Ocean and Caribbean Sea, U.S. Southern Command said it targeted the alleged drug traffickers along known smuggling routes and that “intelligence revealed the vessel’s active involvement in narcotrafficking.”

The military did not provide evidence that the vessel was ferrying drugs. A video posted on X showed a small boat in the water before it was enveloped by an explosion.

President Donald Trump has said the U.S. is in “armed conflict” with cartels in Latin America and he has sought to justify the attacks as a necessary escalation to stem the flow of drugs into the United States and fatal overdoses claiming American lives. But his administration has offered little evidence to support its claims of killing “narcoterrorists.”

Critics have questioned the overall legality of the boat strikes as well as their effectiveness, in part because the fentanyl behind many fatal overdoses is typically trafficked to the U.S. over land from Mexico, where it is produced with chemicals imported from China and India.

The attacks have drawn intense scrutiny from some Democratic lawmakers and military legal scholars. The Pentagon’s watchdog said in May that it plans to look into whether the U.S. military followed an established targeting framework when carrying out the lethal operations, which include a military commander’s intent, target development and execution. But the evaluation will not probe the legality of the strikes.

Tuesday's strike is among a few that have followed Secretary of State Marco Rubio's pledge in September to seek the approval of U.S. allies in the region for carrying out such attacks. Rubio told reporters that while the U.S. has “the capacity to act unilaterally,” it would rather work with its allies because that is “the most effective way to do it.”

Rubio's statements in Peru last month appeared to signal a shift in strategy. However, Rubio also said the U.S. military would “still blow up ships if need be” and the approach would be “a strike-by-strike or operation-by-operation determination.”

entries.title: Democrats’ Final Pitch on SNAP: ‘Restore Every Dollar’
entries.summary: Democrats are promising a legislative push to restore previous funding levels for SNAP.
entries.content:
Democrats running in some of the most competitive House districts say they’d make restoring federal funds to food aid a top priority if they win control of Congress.

The Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program has become a key part of Democratic messaging around affordability and economic concerns. The Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee put out mobile billboards targeting vulnerable Republicans in Arizona, Colorado, Pennsylvania, New York and Texas over their votes for last year’s reconciliation bill, which cut SNAP funding. Beyond dinging their opponents, multiple Democratic candidates are promising to bring those funds back.

“Restoring SNAP funding is a top priority because this is about feeding kids,” Lindsay James, the Democratic nominee in Iowa’s 2nd Congressional District, told The Washington Sun. “This is about making sure that hard-working families in my state and in this district have the support that they need to build the life that we know their kids deserve.”

SNAP, the largest anti-hunger federal program in the nation, is set to lose about $187 billion in federal funding over the next decade, according to the Congressional Budget Office. The reconciliation bill also increased requirements for participants and shifted costs to states. Since that bill became law, participation has fallen by more than 5.5 million people, including an estimated 2 million children, according to the Center on Budget and Policy Priorities, a left-leaning think tank.

James’ Republican opponent, former state Rep. Joe Mitchell, was not in the House during the reconciliation vote, but the Democrat is still attacking him over cuts she says make working families and children more vulnerable to hunger. Mitchell did not respond to a request for comment. (Republican Rep. Ashley Hinson, who did vote for the reconciliation bill, is vacating the seat to run for the Senate.)

Manny Rutinel, the Democrat running for Colorado’s 8th Congressional District, is also using SNAP cuts to go after his Republican opponent, Rep. Gabe Evans, and his support for the legislation and the Trump administration’s policies.

President Donald Trump and Evans “cut SNAP and took food away from hungry children to give tax cuts to their billionaire donors,” Rutinel told The Sun in a statement.

Evans did not respond to a request for comment. White House spokesperson Anna Kelly defended the SNAP changes in the reconciliation package, saying the law “prioritizes American citizens, and implements reasonable cost-sharing measures with states to crack down on waste, fraud, and abuse.”

Democrats say they have a plan for SNAP beyond attacking their opponents' vote for the legislation.

“Democrats must prioritize reversing SNAP cuts and cutting burdensome red tape on the program that make the process impossible to navigate,” JoAnna Mendoza, the Democrat running to unseat Republican Rep. Juan Ciscomani in Arizona, told The Sun in a statement.

Arizona has seen the largest decline in participation of any state, with enrollment dropping nearly 51% from July 2025 to July 2026, according to U.S. Department of Agriculture data. Arizona’s SNAP agency has said much of the decrease stems from the state’s struggles to implement the new federal requirements for the program. Ciscomani, who also voted for the package, did not respond to a request for comment.

Democrat Bob Brooks, who is challenging Republican Rep. Ryan Mackenzie in Pennsylvania, said Democrats are better positioned to address and reverse the cuts.

“We need more people in Congress who actually understand the challenges working people are facing,” Brooks told The Sun. “This issue isn’t a hypothetical to me. I understand it, because I’ve lived it myself. I’ve relied on food stamps to put food on the table.”

“I’ll push to restore every dollar of SNAP… funding that Mackenzie voted to slash,” Brooks said.

Mackenzie did not respond to a request for comment.

The farm bill could address some of Democrats’ concerns, particularly on costs shifting to states. But the Senate still needs to make a deal, and Democrats are considering alternatives to reverse some cuts.

“I am going to continue pushing to pass my legislation to reverse the Republican cuts so our brothers and sisters can access the support they need,” Sen. Ben Ray Luján (D-New Mexico), ranking member of the Senate Agriculture subcommittee on food and nutrition, told The Sun in a statement.

entries.title: Robert White Is Rushing to Preserve His Eligibility in the D.C. Delegate Race
entries.summary: The Democratic nominee to be the District’s nonvoting congressional delegate is currently exploring options to navigate a 1970 law that threatens his eligibility.
entries.content:
D.C. Council member Robert White, the Democratic nominee for the District’s nonvoting congressional delegate, is racing against the clock to navigate a 1970 law that threatens his eligibility for the seat, telling The Washington Sun on Tuesday that his team is working “through a few options” to resolve the issue.

The obscure provision mandates that the D.C. House delegate cannot hold any other paid public office, such as a D.C. Council seat, at the time of their election. Pushing back on claims that the issue caught his campaign off guard, White told The Sun, “This isn’t new to me. We’ve had a legal theory on this for quite some time.”

But White noted that he recently received a reading on the matter from the D.C. attorney general that he did not agree with and didn’t expect. He added that his team is waiting on additional clarity before sharing a final plan.

The issue was first reported by City Cast D.C. and The Washington Post.

Sign up for The Washington Sun Metro newsletter for essential coverage of the D.C. region.

With the general election approaching on Nov. 3, White appeared set for a steady path to succeed outgoing Delegate Eleanor Holmes Norton after winning the June Democratic primary. Now, he faces a tight deadline to either resign from the council and forfeit his final months in the role or persuade his colleagues to consider changing the law before Tuesday, which would require emergency action from the council.

Sarah Graham, a spokeswoman for D.C.’s Board of Elections, stated that White is eligible to run for delegate under the current law so long as he resigns before Election Day next week.

Despite the looming deadline, White signaled he is undeterred and fully preparing to take office. He told The Sun that he spent Tuesday calling incoming members from solidly Democratic districts to introduce himself, offer to be a resource and ensure they understand D.C. home rule.

“We’ve got to address it,” White said. “I’ve got a few days to make a call and determination, but I’m not going to jeopardize going into Congress.”

White participated in a debate on Friday during which he outlined an aggressive take on the delegate role, including fighting for D.C. statehood and preventing congressional interference in local affairs.

The statutory restriction dates back to 1970, when Congress first passed legislation to create the nonvoting delegate position for the District.

entries.title: Supreme Court Declines to Bring Back Biden-Era Immigration Rule
entries.summary: Three cities sought to undo a judgment they said was the result of collusion between the Justice Department and Texas.
entries.content:
The Supreme Court on Tuesday declined to revive a Biden-era rule allowing immigration judges to close deportation proceedings for people who are in the process of obtaining lawful status.

The one-line order comes almost two weeks after three cities and a California legal aid group petitioned the justices to restore the rule, arguing that the Justice Department and Texas colluded to eliminate it outside of the established rulemaking process.

At issue is a June judgment halting the rule nationwide. A federal judge in Texas entered it on the same day the state filed a lawsuit against the Justice Department. The Trump administration and Texas jointly asked the court to bar the immigration court system from ever enacting a similar policy.

In an application to the justices, Baltimore; Columbus, Ohio; New Haven, Connecticut; and Centro Legal de la Raza argued that the judgment erased certain important procedures, “over the course of a single day, without meaningful judicial review, public participation” or rulemaking requirements.

The blocked rule had given immigration judges discretion to spare victims of crimes or neglected children from facing deportation proceedings while undergoing a process to gain immigration relief from U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services, the application says.

The Supreme Court decided to let the judgment stand while the legal case plays out. The Justice Department and Texas argued in filings last week that the cities and Centro Legal de la Raza lacked the right to intervene.

“A stay would revive a rule the district court declared unlawful, renew the fiscal and sovereign injuries Texas alleged, and unsettle a final judgment accepted by the actual parties,” Texas’ court filing last week states. “It would also restore a binding regulation that the Federal Government would have to administer unless and until lawfully displaced, even though responsible officials concluded that the Rule cannot be defended in good faith.”
